### 1926–1943: Family and education
[edit]
Anthony Dominick Benedetto was born on August 3, 1926,[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-bio.com-4) at St. John's Hospital in Long Island City, Queens, in New York City.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-5) His parents were grocer John Benedetto and seamstress Anna (née Suraci), and he was the first member of his family to be born in a hospital.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-evanier-22-6) In 1906, John had emigrated from Podargoni, a rural eastern district of the southern Italian city of Reggio Calabria; he was a member of the local ethnic Greek community (Griko people).[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-evanier-29-7) Anna had been born in the U.S. shortly after her parents also emigrated from the Calabria region in 1899.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-evanier-22-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-evanier-29-7) Other relatives were also part of the mass migration of Italians to America.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-evanier-22-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-evanier-29-7) Tony grew up with an older sister, Mary, and an older brother, John Jr.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-8) With a father who was ailing and unable to work, the children grew up in poverty.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-sullivan-9) John Sr.

### 1926–1943: Family and education
instilled in his son a love of art and literature, and a compassion for human suffering,[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-10) but died when Tony was ten years old.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-sullivan-9)
Bennett grew up listening to Al Jolson, Eddie Cantor, Judy Garland, and Bing Crosby, as well as jazz artists such as Louis Armstrong, Jack Teagarden, and Joe Venuti. His uncle Dick was a tap dancer in vaudeville, giving him an early window into show business,[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-npr-jazz-11) and his uncle Frank was the Queens borough library commissioner.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-evanier-27-12) By age 10 he was already singing, and performed at the opening of the Triborough Bridge,[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-amg-bio-13) standing next to MayorFiorello La Guardia, who patted him on the head.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-evanier-27-12) Drawing was another early passion of his;[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-sullivan-9) he became known as the class caricaturist at P.S. 141 and anticipated a career in commercial art.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-evanier-34-14) He began singing for money at the age of 13, performing as a singing waiter in several Italian restaurants around his native Queens.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-evanier-34-14)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-abc092707-15)

### 1926–1943: Family and education
Bennett attended New York's School of Industrial Art, where he studied painting and music,[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-ghk0495-16) and would later appreciate their emphasis on proper technique.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-17) However, he dropped out at the age of 16 to help support his family.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-aarp-18) He worked as a copy boy and runner for the Associated Press in Manhattan[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-19) and in several other low-skilled, low-paying jobs.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-evanier-40-20) He mostly set his sights on a professional singing career, returning to performing as a singing waiter, playing and winning amateur nights all around the city, and enjoying a successful engagement at a Paramus, New Jersey, nightclub.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-abc092707-15)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-evanier-40-20)

### 1944–1950: World War II and after
[edit]
Benedetto was drafted into the United States Army in November 1944, during the final stages of World War II.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-sullivan-9)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-21) He did basic training at Fort Dix and Fort Robinson as part of becoming an infantry rifleman.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-gl-52-22) In January 1945, he was assigned as a replacement infantryman to the 255th Infantry Regiment of the 63rd Infantry Division, a unit filling in for the heavy losses suffered in the Battle of the Bulge.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-gl-55-23) He moved across France and later into Germany.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-sullivan-9) As March 1945 began, he joined the front line of what he would later describe as a "front-row seat in hell".[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-gl-55-23)

### 1944–1950: World War II and after
As the German Army was pushed back to its homeland, Benedetto and his company saw bitter fighting in cold winter conditions, often hunkering down in foxholes as German 88 mm guns fired on them.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-gl-57-24) At the end of March, they crossed the Rhine and entered Germany, engaging in dangerous house-to-house, town-after-town fighting to clean out German soldiers;[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-gl-57-24) during the first week of April, they crossed the Kocher River, and by the end of the month reached the Danube.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-gl-60-25) During his time in combat, Benedetto narrowly escaped death several times.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-sullivan-9) The experience made him a pacifist;[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-sullivan-9) he would later write, "Anybody who thinks that war is romantic obviously hasn't gone through one",[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-gl-55-23) and later say, "It was a nightmare that's permanent. I just said, 'This is not life. This is not life.'"[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-abc-attacks-26) At the war's conclusion he was involved in the liberation of the Kaufering concentration camp, a subcamp of Dachau, near Landsberg, where some American prisoners of war from the 63rd Division had also been held.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-gl-60-25) He later wrote in his autobiography that "I saw things no human being should ever have to see."[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-Time-27)

### 1944–1950: World War II and after
Benedetto stayed in Germany as part of the occupying force but was assigned to an informal Special Services band unit that would entertain nearby American forces.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-sullivan-9) His dining with a black friend from high school—at a time when the Army was still racially segregated—led to his being demoted and reassigned to Graves Registration Service duties.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-tavis-int-28) Subsequently, he sang with the 314th Army Special Services Band under the stage name Joe Bari[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-gl-74-29) (a name he had started using before the war, chosen after the city and province in Italy, and as a partial anagram of his family origins in Calabria).[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-30) He played with many musicians who would have post-war careers.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-gl-74-29)

### 1944–1950: World War II and after
Upon his discharge from the Army and return to the States in 1946, Benedetto studied at the American Theatre Wing on the GI Bill.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-amg-bio-13) He was taught the _bel canto_ singing discipline,[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-ap090507-31) which would keep his voice in good shape for his entire career. He continued to perform wherever he could, including while waiting tables.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-sullivan-9) Based upon a suggestion from a teacher at the American Theatre Wing, he developed an unusual approach that involved imitating, as he sang, the style and phrasing of other musicians—such as that of Stan Getz's saxophone and Art Tatum's piano—helping him to improvise as he interpreted a song.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-aarp-18)[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-32) He made a few recordings as Bari in 1949 for a small outfit called Leslie Records, but they failed to sell.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-cleve-33)
In 1949, Pearl Bailey recognized Benedetto's talent and asked him to open for her in Greenwich Village.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-abc092707-15) She had invited Bob Hope to the show. Hope decided to take Benedetto on the road with him and shortened his name to Tony Bennett.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-cleve-33) In 1950, Bennett cut a demo of "Boulevard of Broken Dreams" and was signed to the major label Columbia Records by Mitch Miller.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-amg-bio-13)

### 1951–1959: First successes
[edit]
Bennett (right) with Chicago columnist and talk show host Irv Kupcinet, during the 1950s
Warned by Miller not to imitate Frank Sinatra[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-npr-jazz-11) (who was just then leaving Columbia), Bennett began his career as a crooner of commercial pop tunes. His first big hit was "Because of You", a ballad produced by Miller with a lush orchestral arrangement by Percy Faith. It began gaining popularity on jukeboxes, then reached number one on the pop charts in 1951 and stayed there for ten weeks,[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-essential-34) selling over a million copies.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-cleve-33) This was followed to the top of the charts later that year[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-essential-34) by a similarly styled rendition of Hank Williams's "Cold, Cold Heart", which helped introduce Williams and country music in general to a wider national audience.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-35) The Miller and Faith team continued to work on all of Bennett's early hits. Bennett's recording of "Blue Velvet" was also very popular and attracted screaming teenage fans at concerts at the famed Paramount Theater in New York (where Bennett did seven shows a day, starting at 10:30 am)[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-cnn101807-36) and elsewhere.

**Domenico Modugno** (born January 9, 1928 – died August 6, 1994) was a famous Italian singer, songwriter, and actor. Later in his life, he also became a member of the Italian Parliament. He is best known for his huge international hit song from 1958, "Nel blu dipinto di blu" (often called "Volare"). This song won him two Grammy Awards. Many people see him as the first true Italian _cantautore_, which means a singer-songwriter who writes and performs their own songs.

## Domenico Modugno's Early Life
Domenico Modugno was born in Polignano a Mare, Italy, on January 9, 1928. He was the youngest of four children. His father, Vito Cosimo Modugno, worked as a police commander, and his mother, Pasqua Lorusso, was a housewife.
When Domenico was nine, his family moved to San Pietro Vernotico. There, he went to primary school and learned the local dialect. He later attended secondary school in Lecce.

## Domenico Modugno's Music Career
While still a student, Domenico Modugno started acting in films. His first taste of fame came in 1957 when his song "Lazzarella" placed second in a big Italian music contest called the Festival della Canzone Napoletana.
The biggest moment of his career happened in 1958. He entered the Sanremo Music Festival with a song he co-wrote called "Nel blu dipinto di blu". This song won the contest and became a massive hit all over the world. It sold over 22 million copies and won two Grammy Awards. The song also represented Italy in the 1958 Eurovision Song Contest, where it finished third.
Domenico Modugno singing "Nel blu, dipinto di blu" at the Eurovision Song Contest 1958.
Modugno won the Sanremo Music Festival again in 1959 with "Piove" (also known as "Ciao, ciao bambina"). He also came in second place in 1960 with "Libero." He represented Italy in the Eurovision Song Contest again in 1959. Later, his song "Io" was covered by Elvis Presley in English, titled "Ask Me."
In 1962, Modugno won the Sanremo Music Festival for a third time with "Addio... addio...." He returned to Eurovision in 1966 with "Dio, come ti amo." Other artists like Sergio Franchi and Jack Jones later recorded this song.
Besides singing, Modugno acted in many movies, appearing in 44 films. He also produced two films, including _Tutto è musica_ (1963), which was about his own life. In the 1970s, he started focusing more on classical music and acting in modern operas.

## Domenico Modugno's Later Years
In 1984, Domenico Modugno had a serious health issue that affected his ability to perform. This led him to focus on his recovery.
From 1986, he became very active in fighting for the rights of people with disabilities. In June 1987, he was elected to the Italian Parliament as a representative for Turin. He was part of the Radical Party, a group focused on social issues. He spoke out against unfair treatment of patients in hospitals and supported campaigns for human rights.
Modugno returned to music in 1992–1993. His last song was "Delfini" (meaning "Dolphins"), which he sang with his son, Massimo, in 1993.
Domenico Modugno passed away on August 6, 1994, at the age of 66. He died from a heart attack at his home on the island of Lampedusa, south of Sicily. His beautiful beach house was later put up for sale.

Here are some of Domenico Modugno's well-known songs:

Title: Francesco Guccini, Italian singer-songwriter, dies aged 86
Chunks: 0,1,2,3
The singer-songwriter **Francesco Guccini died on Thursday morning** in the hamlet of Pavana, in the municipality of Sambuca Pistoiese, at the age of 86.
His family announced his death in an official statement, confirming that the artist passed away surrounded by the love of his wife Raffaella, his daughter Teresa and his relatives.
In accordance with the artist's wishes, **the funeral will take place in the coming days in the strictest privacy**.
"In asking that this moment of grief may be lived in the utmost intimacy, we would like to thank in advance all those who will share in their mourning with affection, discretion and respect", read the family's message.
**A ceremony will be held in September to commemorate** the man who has been described as one of the most influential singer-songwriters in Italian music.

## One of the most influential singer-songwriters in Italian music
Born in Modena on 14 June 1940, Guccini was **deeply attached to his roots and in particular to the land of the Tuscan-Emilian Apennines**.
He spent his childhood in Pavana, his paternal grandparents' village, because of the Second World War. That deep bond with his native land and with the Apennines would go on to shape all of his poetry and his literary output.
After his first musical experiences in the 1950s and a spell as a young reporter at the Gazzetta di Modena, he moved to Bologna in 1961.
**His career took off in the 1960s, initially as a songwriter for performers such as Caterina Caselli, Equipe 84 and I Nomadi,** for whom he wrote benchmark tracks including 'Auschwitz', 'Dio è morto', 'Per fare un uomo' and 'Noi ci saremo'.
His official recording debut came in 1967 with the album **Folk beat n. 1**. In 1972 he released Radici, a record that included landmark songs such as 'La locomotiva', 'Incontro', 'Il vecchio e il bambino' and 'Piccola città'.
But commercial success arrived **in 1976 with the album Via Paolo Fabbri 43**, a blues record that evokes Bologna's nights and the atmosphere of the time.

### 1926–1943: Family and education
[edit]
Anthony Dominick Benedetto was born on August 3, 1926,[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-bio.com-4) at St. John's Hospital in Long Island City, Queens, in New York City.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-5) His parents were grocer John Benedetto and seamstress Anna (née Suraci), and he was the first member of his family to be born in a hospital.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-evanier-22-6) In 1906, John had emigrated from Podargoni, a rural eastern district of the southern Italian city of Reggio Calabria; he was a member of the local ethnic Greek community (Griko people).[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-evanier-29-7) Anna had been born in the U.S. shortly after her parents also emigrated from the Calabria region in 1899.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-evanier-22-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-evanier-29-7) Other relatives were also part of the mass migration of Italians to America.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-evanier-22-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-evanier-29-7) Tony grew up with an older sister, Mary, and an older brother, John Jr.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-8) With a father who was ailing and unable to work, the children grew up in poverty.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-sullivan-9) John Sr.

### 1926–1943: Family and education

Bennett grew up listening to Al Jolson, Eddie Cantor, Judy Garland, and Bing Crosby, as well as jazz artists such as Louis Armstrong, Jack Teagarden, and Joe Venuti. His uncle Dick was a tap dancer in vaudeville, giving him an early window into show business,[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-npr-jazz-11) and his uncle Frank was the Queens borough library commissioner.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-evanier-27-12) By age 10 he was already singing, and performed at the opening of the Triborough Bridge,[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-amg-bio-13) standing next to MayorFiorello La Guardia, who patted him on the head.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-evanier-27-12) Drawing was another early passion of his;[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-sullivan-9) he became known as the class caricaturist at P.S. 141 and anticipated a career in commercial art.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-evanier-34-14) He began singing for money at the age of 13, performing as a singing waiter in several Italian restaurants around his native Queens.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-evanier-34-14)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-abc092707-15)

### 1926–1943: Family and education
Bennett attended New York's School of Industrial Art, where he studied painting and music,[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-ghk0495-16) and would later appreciate their emphasis on proper technique.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-17) However, he dropped out at the age of 16 to help support his family.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-aarp-18) He worked as a copy boy and runner for the Associated Press in Manhattan[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-19) and in several other low-skilled, low-paying jobs.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-evanier-40-20) He mostly set his sights on a professional singing career, returning to performing as a singing waiter, playing and winning amateur nights all around the city, and enjoying a successful engagement at a Paramus, New Jersey, nightclub.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-abc092707-15)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-evanier-40-20)

### 1944–1950: World War II and after
[edit]
Benedetto was drafted into the United States Army in November 1944, during the final stages of World War II.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-sullivan-9)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-21) He did basic training at Fort Dix and Fort Robinson as part of becoming an infantry rifleman.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-gl-52-22) In January 1945, he was assigned as a replacement infantryman to the 255th Infantry Regiment of the 63rd Infantry Division, a unit filling in for the heavy losses suffered in the Battle of the Bulge.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-gl-55-23) He moved across France and later into Germany.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-sullivan-9) As March 1945 began, he joined the front line of what he would later describe as a "front-row seat in hell".[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-gl-55-23)
texts.7:
### 1944–1950: World War II and after
As the German Army was pushed back to its homeland, Benedetto and his company saw bitter fighting in cold winter conditions, often hunkering down in foxholes as German 88 mm guns fired on them.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-gl-57-24) At the end of March, they crossed the Rhine and entered Germany, engaging in dangerous house-to-house, town-after-town fighting to clean out German soldiers;[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-gl-57-24) during the first week of April, they crossed the Kocher River, and by the end of the month reached the Danube.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-gl-60-25) During his time in combat, Benedetto narrowly escaped death several times.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-sullivan-9) The experience made him a pacifist;[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-sullivan-9) he would later write, "Anybody who thinks that war is romantic obviously hasn't gone through one",[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-gl-55-23) and later say, "It was a nightmare that's permanent. I just said, 'This is not life. This is not life.'"[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-abc-attacks-26) At the war's conclusion he was involved in the liberation of the Kaufering concentration camp, a subcamp of Dachau, near Landsberg, where some American prisoners of war from the 63rd Division had also been held.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-gl-60-25) He later wrote in his autobiography that "I saw things no human being should ever have to see."[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-Time-27)
texts.8:
### 1944–1950: World War II and after
Benedetto stayed in Germany as part of the occupying force but was assigned to an informal Special Services band unit that would entertain nearby American forces.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-sullivan-9) His dining with a black friend from high school—at a time when the Army was still racially segregated—led to his being demoted and reassigned to Graves Registration Service duties.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-tavis-int-28) Subsequently, he sang with the 314th Army Special Services Band under the stage name Joe Bari[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-gl-74-29) (a name he had started using before the war, chosen after the city and province in Italy, and as a partial anagram of his family origins in Calabria).[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-30) He played with many musicians who would have post-war careers.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-gl-74-29)

### 1944–1950: World War II and after
Upon his discharge from the Army and return to the States in 1946, Benedetto studied at the American Theatre Wing on the GI Bill.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-amg-bio-13) He was taught the _bel canto_ singing discipline,[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-ap090507-31) which would keep his voice in good shape for his entire career. He continued to perform wherever he could, including while waiting tables.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-sullivan-9) Based upon a suggestion from a teacher at the American Theatre Wing, he developed an unusual approach that involved imitating, as he sang, the style and phrasing of other musicians—such as that of Stan Getz's saxophone and Art Tatum's piano—helping him to improvise as he interpreted a song.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-aarp-18)[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-32) He made a few recordings as Bari in 1949 for a small outfit called Leslie Records, but they failed to sell.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-cleve-33)
In 1949, Pearl Bailey recognized Benedetto's talent and asked him to open for her in Greenwich Village.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-abc092707-15) She had invited Bob Hope to the show. Hope decided to take Benedetto on the road with him and shortened his name to Tony Bennett.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-cleve-33) In 1950, Bennett cut a demo of "Boulevard of Broken Dreams" and was signed to the major label Columbia Records by Mitch Miller.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-amg-bio-13)
texts.10:
### 1951–1959: First successes
[edit]
Bennett (right) with Chicago columnist and talk show host Irv Kupcinet, during the 1950s
Warned by Miller not to imitate Frank Sinatra[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-npr-jazz-11) (who was just then leaving Columbia), Bennett began his career as a crooner of commercial pop tunes. His first big hit was "Because of You", a ballad produced by Miller with a lush orchestral arrangement by Percy Faith. It began gaining popularity on jukeboxes, then reached number one on the pop charts in 1951 and stayed there for ten weeks,[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-essential-34) selling over a million copies.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-cleve-33) This was followed to the top of the charts later that year[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-essential-34) by a similarly styled rendition of Hank Williams's "Cold, Cold Heart", which helped introduce Williams and country music in general to a wider national audience.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-35) The Miller and Faith team continued to work on all of Bennett's early hits. Bennett's recording of "Blue Velvet" was also very popular and attracted screaming teenage fans at concerts at the famed Paramount Theater in New York (where Bennett did seven shows a day, starting at 10:30 am)[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-cnn101807-36) and elsewhere.

**Domenico Modugno** (born January 9, 1928 – died August 6, 1994) was a famous Italian singer, songwriter, and actor. Later in his life, he also became a member of the Italian Parliament. He is best known for his huge international hit song from 1958, "Nel blu dipinto di blu" (often called "Volare"). This song won him two Grammy Awards. Many people see him as the first true Italian _cantautore_, which means a singer-songwriter who writes and performs their own songs.

## Domenico Modugno's Early Life
Domenico Modugno was born in Polignano a Mare, Italy, on January 9, 1928. He was the youngest of four children. His father, Vito Cosimo Modugno, worked as a police commander, and his mother, Pasqua Lorusso, was a housewife.
When Domenico was nine, his family moved to San Pietro Vernotico. There, he went to primary school and learned the local dialect. He later attended secondary school in Lecce.
texts.3:
## Domenico Modugno's Music Career
While still a student, Domenico Modugno started acting in films. His first taste of fame came in 1957 when his song "Lazzarella" placed second in a big Italian music contest called the Festival della Canzone Napoletana.
The biggest moment of his career happened in 1958. He entered the Sanremo Music Festival with a song he co-wrote called "Nel blu dipinto di blu". This song won the contest and became a massive hit all over the world. It sold over 22 million copies and won two Grammy Awards. The song also represented Italy in the 1958 Eurovision Song Contest, where it finished third.
Domenico Modugno singing "Nel blu, dipinto di blu" at the Eurovision Song Contest 1958.
Modugno won the Sanremo Music Festival again in 1959 with "Piove" (also known as "Ciao, ciao bambina"). He also came in second place in 1960 with "Libero." He represented Italy in the Eurovision Song Contest again in 1959. Later, his song "Io" was covered by Elvis Presley in English, titled "Ask Me."
In 1962, Modugno won the Sanremo Music Festival for a third time with "Addio... addio...." He returned to Eurovision in 1966 with "Dio, come ti amo." Other artists like Sergio Franchi and Jack Jones later recorded this song.
Besides singing, Modugno acted in many movies, appearing in 44 films. He also produced two films, including _Tutto è musica_ (1963), which was about his own life. In the 1970s, he started focusing more on classical music and acting in modern operas.
texts.4:
## Domenico Modugno's Later Years
In 1984, Domenico Modugno had a serious health issue that affected his ability to perform. This led him to focus on his recovery.
From 1986, he became very active in fighting for the rights of people with disabilities. In June 1987, he was elected to the Italian Parliament as a representative for Turin. He was part of the Radical Party, a group focused on social issues. He spoke out against unfair treatment of patients in hospitals and supported campaigns for human rights.
Modugno returned to music in 1992–1993. His last song was "Delfini" (meaning "Dolphins"), which he sang with his son, Massimo, in 1993.
Domenico Modugno passed away on August 6, 1994, at the age of 66. He died from a heart attack at his home on the island of Lampedusa, south of Sicily. His beautiful beach house was later put up for sale.

### 1926–1943: Family and education
[edit]
Anthony Dominick Benedetto was born on August 3, 1926,[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-bio.com-4) at St. John's Hospital in Long Island City, Queens, in New York City.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-5) His parents were grocer John Benedetto and seamstress Anna (née Suraci), and he was the first member of his family to be born in a hospital.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-evanier-22-6) In 1906, John had emigrated from Podargoni, a rural eastern district of the southern Italian city of Reggio Calabria; he was a member of the local ethnic Greek community (Griko people).[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-evanier-29-7) Anna had been born in the U.S. shortly after her parents also emigrated from the Calabria region in 1899.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-evanier-22-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-evanier-29-7) Other relatives were also part of the mass migration of Italians to America.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-evanier-22-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-evanier-29-7) Tony grew up with an older sister, Mary, and an older brother, John Jr.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-8) With a father who was ailing and unable to work, the children grew up in poverty.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-sullivan-9) John Sr.

### 1926–1943: Family and education
instilled in his son a love of art and literature, and a compassion for human suffering,[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-10) but died when Tony was ten years old.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-sullivan-9)
Bennett grew up listening to Al Jolson, Eddie Cantor, Judy Garland, and Bing Crosby, as well as jazz artists such as Louis Armstrong, Jack Teagarden, and Joe Venuti. His uncle Dick was a tap dancer in vaudeville, giving him an early window into show business,[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-npr-jazz-11) and his uncle Frank was the Queens borough library commissioner.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-evanier-27-12) By age 10 he was already singing, and performed at the opening of the Triborough Bridge,[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-amg-bio-13) standing next to MayorFiorello La Guardia, who patted him on the head.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-evanier-27-12) Drawing was another early passion of his;[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-sullivan-9) he became known as the class caricaturist at P.S. 141 and anticipated a career in commercial art.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-evanier-34-14) He began singing for money at the age of 13, performing as a singing waiter in several Italian restaurants around his native Queens.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-evanier-34-14)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-abc092707-15)

### 1926–1943: Family and education
Bennett attended New York's School of Industrial Art, where he studied painting and music,[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-ghk0495-16) and would later appreciate their emphasis on proper technique.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-17) However, he dropped out at the age of 16 to help support his family.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-aarp-18) He worked as a copy boy and runner for the Associated Press in Manhattan[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-19) and in several other low-skilled, low-paying jobs.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-evanier-40-20) He mostly set his sights on a professional singing career, returning to performing as a singing waiter, playing and winning amateur nights all around the city, and enjoying a successful engagement at a Paramus, New Jersey, nightclub.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-abc092707-15)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-evanier-40-20)

### 1944–1950: World War II and after
[edit]
Benedetto was drafted into the United States Army in November 1944, during the final stages of World War II.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-sullivan-9)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-21) He did basic training at Fort Dix and Fort Robinson as part of becoming an infantry rifleman.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-gl-52-22) In January 1945, he was assigned as a replacement infantryman to the 255th Infantry Regiment of the 63rd Infantry Division, a unit filling in for the heavy losses suffered in the Battle of the Bulge.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-gl-55-23) He moved across France and later into Germany.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-sullivan-9) As March 1945 began, he joined the front line of what he would later describe as a "front-row seat in hell".[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-gl-55-23)

### 1944–1950: World War II and after
As the German Army was pushed back to its homeland, Benedetto and his company saw bitter fighting in cold winter conditions, often hunkering down in foxholes as German 88 mm guns fired on them.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-gl-57-24) At the end of March, they crossed the Rhine and entered Germany, engaging in dangerous house-to-house, town-after-town fighting to clean out German soldiers;[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-gl-57-24) during the first week of April, they crossed the Kocher River, and by the end of the month reached the Danube.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-gl-60-25) During his time in combat, Benedetto narrowly escaped death several times.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-sullivan-9) The experience made him a pacifist;[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-sullivan-9) he would later write, "Anybody who thinks that war is romantic obviously hasn't gone through one",[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-gl-55-23) and later say, "It was a nightmare that's permanent. I just said, 'This is not life. This is not life.'"[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-abc-attacks-26) At the war's conclusion he was involved in the liberation of the Kaufering concentration camp, a subcamp of Dachau, near Landsberg, where some American prisoners of war from the 63rd Division had also been held.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-gl-60-25) He later wrote in his autobiography that "I saw things no human being should ever have to see."[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-Time-27)

### 1944–1950: World War II and after
Benedetto stayed in Germany as part of the occupying force but was assigned to an informal Special Services band unit that would entertain nearby American forces.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-sullivan-9) His dining with a black friend from high school—at a time when the Army was still racially segregated—led to his being demoted and reassigned to Graves Registration Service duties.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-tavis-int-28) Subsequently, he sang with the 314th Army Special Services Band under the stage name Joe Bari[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-gl-74-29) (a name he had started using before the war, chosen after the city and province in Italy, and as a partial anagram of his family origins in Calabria).[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-30) He played with many musicians who would have post-war careers.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-gl-74-29)

### 1944–1950: World War II and after
Upon his discharge from the Army and return to the States in 1946, Benedetto studied at the American Theatre Wing on the GI Bill.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-amg-bio-13) He was taught the _bel canto_ singing discipline,[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-ap090507-31) which would keep his voice in good shape for his entire career. He continued to perform wherever he could, including while waiting tables.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-sullivan-9) Based upon a suggestion from a teacher at the American Theatre Wing, he developed an unusual approach that involved imitating, as he sang, the style and phrasing of other musicians—such as that of Stan Getz's saxophone and Art Tatum's piano—helping him to improvise as he interpreted a song.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-aarp-18)[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-32) He made a few recordings as Bari in 1949 for a small outfit called Leslie Records, but they failed to sell.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-cleve-33)
In 1949, Pearl Bailey recognized Benedetto's talent and asked him to open for her in Greenwich Village.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-abc092707-15) She had invited Bob Hope to the show. Hope decided to take Benedetto on the road with him and shortened his name to Tony Bennett.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-cleve-33) In 1950, Bennett cut a demo of "Boulevard of Broken Dreams" and was signed to the major label Columbia Records by Mitch Miller.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-amg-bio-13)

### 1951–1959: First successes
[edit]
Bennett (right) with Chicago columnist and talk show host Irv Kupcinet, during the 1950s
Warned by Miller not to imitate Frank Sinatra[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-npr-jazz-11) (who was just then leaving Columbia), Bennett began his career as a crooner of commercial pop tunes. His first big hit was "Because of You", a ballad produced by Miller with a lush orchestral arrangement by Percy Faith. It began gaining popularity on jukeboxes, then reached number one on the pop charts in 1951 and stayed there for ten weeks,[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-essential-34) selling over a million copies.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-cleve-33) This was followed to the top of the charts later that year[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-essential-34) by a similarly styled rendition of Hank Williams's "Cold, Cold Heart", which helped introduce Williams and country music in general to a wider national audience.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-35) The Miller and Faith team continued to work on all of Bennett's early hits. Bennett's recording of "Blue Velvet" was also very popular and attracted screaming teenage fans at concerts at the famed Paramount Theater in New York (where Bennett did seven shows a day, starting at 10:30 am)[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett#cite_note-cnn101807-36) and elsewhere.

**Domenico Modugno** (born January 9, 1928 – died August 6, 1994) was a famous Italian singer, songwriter, and actor. Later in his life, he also became a member of the Italian Parliament. He is best known for his huge international hit song from 1958, "Nel blu dipinto di blu" (often called "Volare"). This song won him two Grammy Awards. Many people see him as the first true Italian _cantautore_, which means a singer-songwriter who writes and performs their own songs.

## Domenico Modugno's Early Life
Domenico Modugno was born in Polignano a Mare, Italy, on January 9, 1928. He was the youngest of four children. His father, Vito Cosimo Modugno, worked as a police commander, and his mother, Pasqua Lorusso, was a housewife.
When Domenico was nine, his family moved to San Pietro Vernotico. There, he went to primary school and learned the local dialect. He later attended secondary school in Lecce.

## Domenico Modugno's Music Career
While still a student, Domenico Modugno started acting in films. His first taste of fame came in 1957 when his song "Lazzarella" placed second in a big Italian music contest called the Festival della Canzone Napoletana.
The biggest moment of his career happened in 1958. He entered the Sanremo Music Festival with a song he co-wrote called "Nel blu dipinto di blu". This song won the contest and became a massive hit all over the world. It sold over 22 million copies and won two Grammy Awards. The song also represented Italy in the 1958 Eurovision Song Contest, where it finished third.
Domenico Modugno singing "Nel blu, dipinto di blu" at the Eurovision Song Contest 1958.
Modugno won the Sanremo Music Festival again in 1959 with "Piove" (also known as "Ciao, ciao bambina"). He also came in second place in 1960 with "Libero." He represented Italy in the Eurovision Song Contest again in 1959. Later, his song "Io" was covered by Elvis Presley in English, titled "Ask Me."
In 1962, Modugno won the Sanremo Music Festival for a third time with "Addio... addio...." He returned to Eurovision in 1966 with "Dio, come ti amo." Other artists like Sergio Franchi and Jack Jones later recorded this song.
Besides singing, Modugno acted in many movies, appearing in 44 films. He also produced two films, including _Tutto è musica_ (1963), which was about his own life. In the 1970s, he started focusing more on classical music and acting in modern operas.

## Domenico Modugno's Later Years
In 1984, Domenico Modugno had a serious health issue that affected his ability to perform. This led him to focus on his recovery.
From 1986, he became very active in fighting for the rights of people with disabilities. In June 1987, he was elected to the Italian Parliament as a representative for Turin. He was part of the Radical Party, a group focused on social issues. He spoke out against unfair treatment of patients in hospitals and supported campaigns for human rights.
Modugno returned to music in 1992–1993. His last song was "Delfini" (meaning "Dolphins"), which he sang with his son, Massimo, in 1993.
Domenico Modugno passed away on August 6, 1994, at the age of 66. He died from a heart attack at his home on the island of Lampedusa, south of Sicily. His beautiful beach house was later put up for sale.

Title: Francesco Guccini, Italian singer-songwriter, dies aged 86
Chunks: 0,1,2,3
The singer-songwriter **Francesco Guccini died on Thursday morning** in the hamlet of Pavana, in the municipality of Sambuca Pistoiese, at the age of 86.
His family announced his death in an official statement, confirming that the artist passed away surrounded by the love of his wife Raffaella, his daughter Teresa and his relatives.
In accordance with the artist's wishes, **the funeral will take place in the coming days in the strictest privacy**.
"In asking that this moment of grief may be lived in the utmost intimacy, we would like to thank in advance all those who will share in their mourning with affection, discretion and respect", read the family's message.
**A ceremony will be held in September to commemorate** the man who has been described as one of the most influential singer-songwriters in Italian music.

## One of the most influential singer-songwriters in Italian music
Born in Modena on 14 June 1940, Guccini was **deeply attached to his roots and in particular to the land of the Tuscan-Emilian Apennines**.
He spent his childhood in Pavana, his paternal grandparents' village, because of the Second World War. That deep bond with his native land and with the Apennines would go on to shape all of his poetry and his literary output.
After his first musical experiences in the 1950s and a spell as a young reporter at the Gazzetta di Modena, he moved to Bologna in 1961.
**His career took off in the 1960s, initially as a songwriter for performers such as Caterina Caselli, Equipe 84 and I Nomadi,** for whom he wrote benchmark tracks including 'Auschwitz', 'Dio è morto', 'Per fare un uomo' and 'Noi ci saremo'.
His official recording debut came in 1967 with the album **Folk beat n. 1**. In 1972 he released Radici, a record that included landmark songs such as 'La locomotiva', 'Incontro', 'Il vecchio e il bambino' and 'Piccola città'.
But commercial success arrived **in 1976 with the album Via Paolo Fabbri 43**, a blues record that evokes Bologna's nights and the atmosphere of the time.
The track 'L'avvelenata', included on the same album, spits anger and pride and responds to the criticism levelled at him in those years by other singer-songwriters.
Then came Amerigo in 1978, featuring the celebrated Eskimo, which earned him the nickname "the singer-songwriter with the eskimo".
In 1981 he released Metropolis, followed by live projects such as Opera buffa and Fra la via Emilia e il West.
At his concerts, music and songs were interwoven with monologues and the tone of the finest cabaret.
His music and writing are rich in cultural references, ranging from Italian poetry to international poetics and essay writing, and to the Bible.
After the release of L'ultima Thule in 2012, Guccini announced that he was retiring from active music-making to devote himself to writing.

## One of the most influential singer-songwriters in Italian music
He subsequently released Canzoni da intorto in 2022 and Canzoni da osteria in 2023.
Over the course of his career he **received numerous awards, including several Targa Tenco and Premio Tenco awards.**

## A career beyond music
A versatile artist and a leading figure in Italy's world of auteur culture, **Guccini was also a writer of non-fiction and novels.**
His narrative debut came in 1989 with **Cròniche epafàniche**, followed by the publication of numerous books, including **Vacca d'un cane** and the series of novels co-written with Loriano Macchiavelli.
**Guccini also taught Italian at Dickinson College in Bologna** from 1965 to 1985, and worked as a screenwriter and comic-book writer, as an actor and as a scholar of dialectology.
In 2002 the University of Bologna awarded him an **honorary degree in Education Sciences**.
In 2020 he was among the finalists for the Premio Campiello with his novel Tralummescuro.

Peppino di Capri, born Giuseppe Faiella, was one of Italy’s most celebrated singers and pianists. He became famous for blending traditional Neapolitan music with rock ‘n’ roll, twist, and Italian pop music. Title: Francesco Calazzo on Instagram: "February 3, 1960.
Exactly one year after the day the music died in the US, Italy lost one of its most magnetic voices.

Fred Buscaglione, né Ferdinando Buscaglione, died tragically in Rome at just 38, cutting short a career that felt as if it was only getting started. A larger-than-life performer with impeccable timing, swagger, and irony, he blended swing, jazz, and pop with a distinctly Italian sense of theatre. Think Louis Prima’s exuberance crossed with Dean Martin’s cool — filtered through post-war Italy.

Buscaglione created characters, not just songs: hard-boiled lovers, night owls, fast cars, smoky bars. Beneath the bravado was a sharp musician and an instinctive showman who understood spectacle long before it became a formula.

His death marked the end of an era that never quite had the time to fully unfold. Like so many others taken too soon, he became frozen in that moment.

Title: Francesco Calazzo on Instagram: "February 3, 1960.
Exactly one year after the day the music died in the US, Italy lost one of its most magnetic voices.

Fred Buscaglione, né Ferdinando Buscaglione, died tragically in Rome at just 38, cutting short a career that felt as if it was only getting started. A larger-than-life performer with impeccable timing, swagger, and irony, he blended swing, jazz, and pop with a distinctly Italian sense of theatre. Think Louis Prima’s exuberance crossed with Dean Martin’s cool — filtered through post-war Italy.

Buscaglione created characters, not just songs: hard-boiled lovers, night owls, fast cars, smoky bars. Beneath the bravado was a sharp musician and an instinctive showman who understood spectacle long before it became a formula.

His death marked the end of an era that never quite had the time to fully unfold. Like so many others taken too soon, he became frozen in that moment.

**Samuel Cooke**[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Cooke#cite_note-britannica-5) (né**Cook**; January 22, 1931[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Cooke#cite_note-6) – December 11, 1964)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Cooke#cite_note-britannica-5) was an American soul singer and songwriter. Considered one of the most influential soul artists of all time, Cooke is commonly referred to as the **"King of Soul"**_[citation needed_] for his distinctive vocals, pioneering contributions to the genre, and significance in popular music.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Cooke#cite_note-7) During his thirteen-year career, Cooke released 29 singles that charted in the Top 40 of the _Billboard_ Hot 100 chart, as well as 20 singles in the Top 10 of _Billboard_'sBlack Singles chart. In 1964, he was shot and killed by the manager of a motel in Los Angeles.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Cooke#cite_note-mofmotl-8) His family has since questioned the circumstances of his death. In 2015, Cooke was ranked number 28 in _Billboard_ magazine's list of the "35 Greatest R&B Artists of All Time" and number 3 in _Rolling Stone_ magazine's list of the "[200 Greatest Singers of All Time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rolling_Stone's_200_Greatest_Singers_of_All_Time "Rolling Stone's 200 Greatest Singers of All Time")", behind only Whitney Houston (number 2) and Aretha Franklin (number 1).[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Cooke#cite_note-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Cooke#cite_note-10)

Sam Cooke was born Samuel Cook in Clarksdale, Mississippi, in 1931 (he added the "e" to his last name in 1958 to signify a new start to his life).[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Cooke#cite_note-Guralnick-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Cooke#cite_note-12) He was the fifth of eight children of Rev. Charles Cook, a Baptist minister, and the former Annie Mae Carroll. One of his younger brothers, L.C. (1932–2017),[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Cooke#cite_note-L.C._Cooke_obi-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Cooke#cite_note-14) later became a member of the doo-wop band Johnny Keyes and the Magnificents.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Cooke#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGuralnick20059%E2%80%9310,_17-15) Cooke was raised Baptist.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Cooke#cite_note-16)

Cooke's family moved to Chicago in 1933.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Cooke#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGuralnick200510-17) There, he attended Doolittle Elementary and Wendell Phillips Academy High School,[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Cooke#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGuralnick200515,_22-18) the same school that Nat King Cole had attended a few years earlier. Cooke sang in the choir of his father's church and began his career with his siblings in a group called the Singing Children when he was six years old.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Cooke#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGuralnick200513%E2%80%9314-19) Cooke first became known as lead singer with [the Highway Q.C.'s](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Highway_Q.C.'s "The Highway Q.C.'s") when he was a teenager, having joined the group at the age of 14.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Cooke#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGuralnick200529%E2%80%9331-20) During this time, Cooke befriended fellow gospel singer and neighbor Lou Rawls, who sang in a rival gospel group.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Cooke#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGuralnick200590-21)
In 1950, Cooke replaced gospel tenor R. H. Harris as lead singer of his gospel group The Soul Stirrers, who had signed with Specialty Records on behalf of the group.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Cooke#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGuralnick200565%E2%80%9368-22)

Their first recording under Cooke's leadership was the song "Jesus Gave Me Water" in 1950. They also recorded the gospel songs "Peace in the Valley", "How Far Am I from Canaan?", "Jesus Paid the Debt" and "One More River", among many others, some of which he wrote.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Cooke#cite_note-songsofsamcooke.com-4)
Cooke was often credited with bringing gospel music to the attention of a younger crowd of listeners, mainly girls who would rush to the stage when the Soul Stirrers hit the stage just to get a glimpse of him.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Cooke#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGuralnick200547-23)
Cooke formally left the Soul Stirrers in 1956 after deciding to pursue a secular career as a solo artist, prompting a backlash from the gospel community and religious leaders.
Prior to leaving the Soul Stirrers in 1956, Cooke recorded his first secular pop song, "Lovable", a remake of the gospel song "Wonderful", under the alias Dale Cook, in hopes of not getting discovered recording secular material because of the stigma against gospel singers performing pop music, which failed due to Cooke's instantly recognizable voice.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Cooke#cite_note-pc17-24)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Cooke#cite_note-bookofhits-25)
Art Rupe, head of Specialty Records, the label of the Soul Stirrers, gave his blessing for Cooke to record secular music under his real name, but he was unhappy about the type of music Cooke and producer Bumps Blackwell were making. Rupe expected Cooke's secular music to be similar to that of another Specialty Records artist, Little Richard. When Rupe walked in on a recording session and heard Cooke singing Gershwin, he was quite upset. After an argument between Rupe and Blackwell, Cooke and Blackwell left the label.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Cooke#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGuralnick2005171%E2%80%93180-26)

Still a relatively new artist, Cooke wanted to branch further from the [Chitlin' Circuit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chitlin'_Circuit "Chitlin' Circuit") and in March 1958, just months after "You Send Me" topped the charts, Cooke booked two weeks at the Copacabana. However, Cooke later said he "bombed" during the residency with many in the audience not being familiar with the singer. Later that year, Cooke performed for the famed Cavalcade of Jazz concert produced by [Leon Hefflin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leon_Hefflin,_Sr. "Leon Hefflin, Sr.") held at the Shrine Auditorium on August 3. The other headliners were Little Willie John, Ray Charles, Ernie Freeman, and Bo Rhambo. [Sammy Davis Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sammy_Davis_Jr. "Sammy Davis Jr.") was there to crown the winner of the Miss Cavalcade of Jazz beauty contest. The event featured the top four prominent disc jockeys of Los Angeles.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Cooke#cite_note-Guralnick-11) By 1959, Cooke sought a new label and wanted to produce his own music, breaking away from Bumps Blackwell after a three-year partnership.
_Billboard_ advertisement, May 29, 1961
In January 1960, Cooke signed a lucrative deal with RCA Victor, having been offered an advance of $100,000 (equivalent to$1.1 million in 2025)[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Cooke#cite_note-inflation-US-31) by the label's producers Hugo & Luigi.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Cooke#cite_note-BbJan60-38)[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Cooke#cite_note-CBJan60-39)

After his first RCA single, "Teenage Sonata", became a relative flop, Keen Records issued the Cooke-produced and co-written "Wonderful World", which reached number 12 on the _Billboard_ Hot 100 and number two on the Hot R&B Sides chart, which changed Cooke's musical direction. Soon after, Cooke released the song "Chain Gang", which peaked at number two on both the _Billboard_ Hot 100 and Hot R&B Sides charts and became his first UK top ten hit.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Cooke#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGuralnick2005338-40) Following this success, Cooke recorded several more hits such as "Cupid", "[Twistin' the Night Away](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twistin'_the_Night_Away "Twistin' the Night Away")", "Bring It On Home to Me" (which featured Lou Rawls in the background), "Having a Party", "Nothing Can Change This Love", "[Send Me Some Lovin'](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Send_Me_Some_Lovin' "Send Me Some Lovin'")" and "Another Saturday Night".[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Cooke#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGuralnick2005348,_361-41)[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Cooke#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGuralnick2005362-42)[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Cooke#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGuralnick2005404%E2%80%93407-43)[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Cooke#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGuralnick2005460-44)[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Cooke#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGuralnick2005390,_396-45) Cooke's 1962 album, _Twistin' the Night Away_, became one of his best selling albums.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Cooke#cite_note-46)

Cooke in _Billboard_, 1965, released posthumously
During this period, Cooke launched his own record label SAR Records with J. W. Alexander and his manager, Roy Crain.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Cooke#cite_note-musichistory-47) The label soon included the Simms Twins, the Valentinos (who were Bobby Womack and his brothers), Mel Carter and Johnnie Taylor. Cooke then created a publishing imprint and management firm named Kags, which made Cooke among the first modern Black performers and composers to attend to the business side of his musical career.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Cooke#cite_note-Goodman-48)
Like most R&B artists of his time, Cooke focused on singles. Cooke was a prolific songwriter and wrote most of the songs he recorded. Cooke also had a hand in overseeing some of the song arrangements. In spite of releasing mostly singles, he released a well-received blues-inflected LP in 1963, _Night Beat_, and his most critically acclaimed studio album, _[Ain't That Good News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ain't\_That\_Good\_News\_(album) "Ain't That Good News (album)")_, which featured five singles, in 1964.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Cooke#cite_note-49) In 1963, Cooke signed a five-year contract for Allen Klein to manage Kags Music and SAR Records, and made him his manager. Klein negotiated a five-year deal (three years plus two option years) with RCA Victor in which a holding company, Tracey, Ltd, named after Cooke's daughter, owned by Klein and managed by J. W. Alexander, would produce and own Cooke's recordings. RCA Victor would get exclusive distribution rights in exchange for six percent royalty payments and payments for the recording sessions.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Cooke#cite_note-inventedsoul-50)

For tax reasons, Cooke would receive preferred stock in Tracey instead of an initial cash advance of $100,000. He would receive cash advances of $100,000 for the next two years, followed by an additional $75,000 for each of the two option years if the deal went to term.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Cooke#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoodman201544%E2%80%9346-51)
In July 1964, Cooke returned to the Copacabana, with his performances there becoming a success due to Cooke now being a more experienced and successful artist. As a result, RCA Victor recorded a live album of one of his Copacabana performances and later released it under the album, _Sam Cooke at the Copa_, which became one of the first number one albums on the R&B Albums chart.
Cooke was known for his tenor voice, which was big, velvety, and expansive, with a recognizable tone. Cooke could go as high as high C without losing purity or volume, and his upper mid-range was coated in a unique rasp. Cooke's vocal style was very adaptable, adopting a rather classical sound on jazz and pop songs while maintaining his trademark stylistic soulful hold on R&B, gospel and soul music.
Cooke's delivery encompassed a wide range of emotions including playful expressiveness to interact with listeners, mellow somberness as a form of reflection, and (in "A Change Is Gonna Come") profound soulfulness. When performing live, he would often play with notes and scales and experiment with melodies and his enunciation, while improvising entire songs. Cooke also began to perform highly charged versions of his songs later in his career.
Cooke's vocal exploits would go on to influence many acts like Otis Redding, James Brown, Rod Stewart, Johnny Nash, Tina Turner, Wilson Pickett, Mick Jagger, Al Green, Paul McCartney, Diana Ross, Marvin Gaye, Steve Perry, and Stevie Wonder among many others.

Cooke was married twice.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Cooke#cite_note-Ebony-52) His first marriage was to singer-dancer Dolores Elizabeth Milligan Cooke, who took the stage name "Dee Dee Mohawk" in 1953; they divorced in 1958.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Cooke#cite_note-:0-53)[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Cooke#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGuralnick2005101,_105-54) She was killed in an auto collision in Fresno, California, in 1959.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Cooke#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGuralnick2005282-55) Although Cooke and Milligan were divorced,[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Cooke#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGuralnick2005243-56) he paid for his ex-wife's funeral expenses.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Cooke#cite_note-:0-53)[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Cooke#cite_note-Ebony-52)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Cooke#cite_note-Guralnick-11)

In 1958, Cooke married his second wife, Barbara Campbell (1935–2021), in Chicago.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Cooke#cite_note-:0-53)[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Cooke#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGuralnick2005303-57) His father performed the ceremony.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Cooke#cite_note-:0-53) They had three children: Linda (b. 1953),[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Cooke#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGuralnick2005102-58) Tracy (b. 1960), and Vincent (1961–1963), who drowned in the family swimming pool.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Cooke#cite_note-Ebony-52)[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Cooke#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGuralnick2005412,_499%E2%80%93500-59)[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Cooke#cite_note-:0-53) Cooke also fathered at least three other children out of wedlock.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Cooke#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGuralnick2005217,_229,_381,_389-60) In 1958, a woman in Philadelphia, Connie Bolling,[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Cooke#cite_note-Guralnick-11) said Cooke was the father of her son. Cooke paid her an estimated $5,000 settlement out of court.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Cooke#cite_note-:0-53)

In November 1958, Cooke was involved in a car crash en route from St. Louis to Greenville, Mississippi. His chauffeur Edward Cunningham was killed, while Cooke, guitarist Cliff White, and singer Lou Rawls were hospitalized.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Cooke#cite_note-:0-53)
Cooke was a central part of the civil rights movement, using his influence and popularity with the White and Black populations to fight for the cause. Cooke was friends with boxer Muhammad Ali, activist Malcolm X and football player Jim Brown, who together campaigned for racial equality.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Cooke#cite_note-61)

## Murder and investigation
[edit]
Cooke was shot and killed on December 11, 1964, at the Hacienda Motel at 91st and South Figueroa streets in South Central Los Angeles. Answering separate reports of a shooting and a kidnapping at the motel, police found Cooke's body. He had sustained a gunshot wound to the chest, which was later determined to have pierced his heart.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Cooke#cite_note-62)
The motel's manager, Bertha Franklin, said she shot Cooke in self-defense. Her account was immediately disputed by Cooke's friends, who were not there at the time of the incident.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Cooke#cite_note-63)[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Cooke#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoodman201557-64) The motel's owner, Evelyn Carr,[[note 1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Cooke#cite_note-65) said that she had been on the telephone with Franklin at the time of the incident. Carr said she overheard Cooke's intrusion and the ensuing conflict and gunshot, and called the police.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Cooke#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGuralnick2005619-66)
The police record states that Franklin fatally shot Cooke, who had checked in earlier that evening.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Cooke#cite_note-Wolff-67) Franklin said Cooke had banged on the door of her office, shouting "Where's the girl?!" in reference to Elisa Boyer, a woman who had accompanied Cooke to the motel and who had called the police that night from a telephone booth near the motel minutes before Carr had.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Cooke#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGuralnick2005619,_627-68)

## NEW 📀 Chapel Of Love - The Dixie Cups {Stereo} Summer 1964
1964......#1 U.S. Billboard Hot 100, #1 U.S. Cash Box Top 100, #1 Canada Original video edited and AI remastered with HQ stereo sound. "Chapel of Love" is a song written by Jeff Barry, Ellie Greenwich and Phil Spector, and made famous by The Dixie Cups in 1964, spending three weeks at number one on the Billboard Hot 100. The song tells of the happiness and excitement the narrator feels on her wedding day, for she and her love are going to the "chapel of love", and "[they'll] never be lonely anymore." Many other artists have recorded the song. It was originally recorded by Darlene Love in April 1963, but her version was not released until 1991. The Dixie Cups' version was the debut release of the new Red Bird Records run by Jerry Leiber and Mike Stoller along with George Goldner. The Ronettes included the song on their debut album released in November 1964 with production by Phil Spector. In 1973, singer and actress Bette Midler had a moderate hit with a cover of "Chapel of Love". The song was written in 1963 by Jeff Barry and Ellie Greenwich, who had themselves recently married; Barry later said that "the concept of marriage was very much in my head" at the time. It was written for Darlene Love to record, but producer Phil Spector was dissatisfied with her version and it was not released for some years. The Mel-Tones – a group of three young women from New Orleans, Barbara Ann Hawkins, Rosa Lee Hawkins, and Joan Marie Johnson – had traveled to New York City with their manager Joe Jones to attempt to get a record deal. They were given the song "Chapel of Love" to sing, and passed an audition with Leiber and Stoller in the Brill Building. The group rehearsed the song with Barry and Greenwich before recording it. The arrangement was by Wardell Quezergue, and Leiber and Stoller added lyrics and some touches to the arrangements.
