# Domenico Modugno
**Domenico Modugno** (Italian pronunciation:[[doˈmeːniko moˈduɲɲo]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Italian "Help:IPA/Italian"); 9 January 1928 – 6 August 1994) was an Italian singer, songwriter, actor and, later in life, a member of the Italian Parliament. He is known for his 1958 international hit song "Nel blu dipinto di blu", for which he received the first Grammy Awards for Record of the Year and Song of the Year. He is considered the first Italian cantautore.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domenico_Modugno#cite_note-bio-1)

# Domenico Modugno
## Early life
[edit]
The youngest of four children, Modugno was born at Polignano a Mare, in the province of Bari (Apulia), on 9 January 1928.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domenico_Modugno#cite_note-Parents-2) His father, Vito Cosimo Modugno,[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domenico_Modugno#cite_note-Birth-3) was a municipal police commander,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domenico_Modugno#cite_note-Parents-2) while his mother, Pasqua Lorusso,[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domenico_Modugno#cite_note-Birth-3) was a housewife.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domenico_Modugno#cite_note-Parents-2)
At the age of 9, his family moved to San Pietro Vernotico, in the Province of Brindisi,[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domenico_Modugno#cite_note-4) where his father was transferred for a new job position.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domenico_Modugno#cite_note-5) Here Domenico attended primary school and learned San Pietro Vernotico's dialect, which belongs to the linguistic area of Salentino dialect, similar to Sicilian. He attended secondary school in Lecce.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domenico_Modugno#cite_note-bio-1)

# Domenico Modugno
## Career
[edit]
Modugno in 1955
[](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Modugno_durante_l'esibizione_al_Festival_di_sanremo_del_1958.jpg)
Modugno opens his arms while performing "Nel blu, dipinto di blu" (better known as "Volare") at the 1958 Sanremo Music Festival
While still studying, Modugno had a role in a cinematographic version of _Filumena Marturano_ by Eduardo De Filippo as well as some other films.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domenico_Modugno#cite_note-bio-1) In 1957, his song "Lazzarella", sung by Aurelio Fierro, came second in the Festival della Canzone Napoletana, bringing him his first taste of popularity.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domenico_Modugno#cite_note-bio-1)
In 1958, Modugno took part in Antonio Aniante's comedy _La Rosa di Zolfo_ at the Festival della Prosa in Venice. Also in 1958, he discovered the Italian comedy duo of Franco and Ciccio, became their manager and got them into a long-running film career.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domenico_Modugno#cite_note-6) The turning point of his career came in that year, when he also participated in the Sanremo Music Festival, presenting, together with Johnny Dorelli, the song "Nel blu dipinto di blu." Co-authored by Modugno and Franco Migliacci, the song won the contest and became an enormous success worldwide. It received two Grammy Awards[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domenico_Modugno#cite_note-NME_Rock_'N'_Roll_Years-7) with sales above 22 million copies, and represented Italy in the Eurovision Song Contest 1958, where it came in third.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domenico_Modugno#cite_note-bio-1)
Modugno reportedly used the money gained with "Nel blu dipinto di blu" to purchase a Ferrari; however, his car was totalled in an accident, which included his fenders being smashed. This was mentioned in the Allan Sherman song "America's a nice Italian Name".

# Domenico Modugno
## Career
In 1959, Modugno won the Sanremo Music Festival for the second time in a row, with "Piove" (also known as "Ciao, ciao bambina"), and received second place in 1960 with "Libero". This was a successful period of time for Modugno who again represented Italy in the Eurovision Song Contest of 1959. Later his hit song "Io" was sung by Elvis Presley in English with the title "Ask Me".[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domenico_Modugno#cite_note-bio-1)
In 1962, Modugno won the Sanremo Music Festival a third time with "Addio..., addio...." Four years later, he again represented Italy at Eurovision with "Dio, come ti amo". Sergio Franchi recorded it in Italian (titled "Oh How Much I Love You (Dio, come ti amo!)) on his 1967 RCA Victor album, _From Sergio-with Love_. Jack Jones recorded it in English for his 1967 album, _Our Song_, under the title "Oh How Much I Love You".[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domenico_Modugno#cite_note-bio-1)Shirley Bassey also recorded it with the title _Oh God How Much I Love You_, on her album _Keep the Music Playing_ in 1991.
Modugno was an actor in 44 movies (such as _Appuntamento a Ischia_), and was a film producer of two (_Tutto è musica_ of 1963 was his own biographical production).[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domenico_Modugno#cite_note-bio-1)
In 1970, Modugno focused on more classic music genres and profiles, as a singer and as a musician, adapting poetry, acting on television and in lead singing roles in modern operas.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domenico_Modugno#cite_note-bio-1)

# Domenico Modugno
## Final years
[edit]
In 1984, Modugno suffered a severe stroke and remained partially paralyzed; this forced him to abandon his artistic career and devote himself to rehab.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domenico_Modugno#cite_note-bio-1)
From 1986, he worked for the rights of disabled people, and in June 1987, he was elected congressman for Turin in the Italian Parliament, in the ranks of the Radical Party, a liberal-social political group.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domenico_Modugno#cite_note-bio-1) In the past, he had supported the campaigns of the Italian Socialist Party and one for divorce, in addition to criticizing the human rights violations by the regime of Augusto Pinochet, that cost him a denial of entry in Chile, where he had been scheduled to hold a concert.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domenico_Modugno#cite_note-bio-1) In this last stage of his life, instead, he was very active in social issues, fighting against the inhumane conditions of patients in the Agrigentopsychiatric hospital.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domenico_Modugno#cite_note-bio-1)
Modugno returned to the music scene, definitively (he already held a concert for former inmates of Agrigento's mental asylum, in 1989), in 1992–1993. His last song was _Delfini_ (_Dolphins_), in 1993 with his son, Massimo.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domenico_Modugno#cite_note-bio-1)

**Domenico Modugno** (born January 9, 1928 – died August 6, 1994) was a famous Italian singer, songwriter, and actor. Later in his life, he also became a member of the Italian Parliament. He is best known for his huge international hit song from 1958, "Nel blu dipinto di blu" (often called "Volare"). This song won him two Grammy Awards. Many people see him as the first true Italian _cantautore_, which means a singer-songwriter who writes and performs their own songs.

## Domenico Modugno's Early Life
Domenico Modugno was born in Polignano a Mare, Italy, on January 9, 1928. He was the youngest of four children. His father, Vito Cosimo Modugno, worked as a police commander, and his mother, Pasqua Lorusso, was a housewife.
When Domenico was nine, his family moved to San Pietro Vernotico. There, he went to primary school and learned the local dialect. He later attended secondary school in Lecce.

## Domenico Modugno's Music Career
While still a student, Domenico Modugno started acting in films. His first taste of fame came in 1957 when his song "Lazzarella" placed second in a big Italian music contest called the Festival della Canzone Napoletana.
The biggest moment of his career happened in 1958. He entered the Sanremo Music Festival with a song he co-wrote called "Nel blu dipinto di blu". This song won the contest and became a massive hit all over the world. It sold over 22 million copies and won two Grammy Awards. The song also represented Italy in the 1958 Eurovision Song Contest, where it finished third.
Domenico Modugno singing "Nel blu, dipinto di blu" at the Eurovision Song Contest 1958.
Modugno won the Sanremo Music Festival again in 1959 with "Piove" (also known as "Ciao, ciao bambina"). He also came in second place in 1960 with "Libero." He represented Italy in the Eurovision Song Contest again in 1959. Later, his song "Io" was covered by Elvis Presley in English, titled "Ask Me."
In 1962, Modugno won the Sanremo Music Festival for a third time with "Addio... addio...." He returned to Eurovision in 1966 with "Dio, come ti amo." Other artists like Sergio Franchi and Jack Jones later recorded this song.
Besides singing, Modugno acted in many movies, appearing in 44 films. He also produced two films, including _Tutto è musica_ (1963), which was about his own life. In the 1970s, he started focusing more on classical music and acting in modern operas.

## Domenico Modugno's Later Years
In 1984, Domenico Modugno had a serious health issue that affected his ability to perform. This led him to focus on his recovery.
From 1986, he became very active in fighting for the rights of people with disabilities. In June 1987, he was elected to the Italian Parliament as a representative for Turin. He was part of the Radical Party, a group focused on social issues. He spoke out against unfair treatment of patients in hospitals and supported campaigns for human rights.
Modugno returned to music in 1992–1993. His last song was "Delfini" (meaning "Dolphins"), which he sang with his son, Massimo, in 1993.
Domenico Modugno passed away on August 6, 1994, at the age of 66. He died from a heart attack at his home on the island of Lampedusa, south of Sicily. His beautiful beach house was later put up for sale.

## Domenico Modugno's Songs
Here are some of Domenico Modugno's well-known songs:

*   "Nel blu dipinto di blu" – also known as "Volare" (Sanremo winner, 1958)

# Domenico Modugno
**Domenico Modugno** (Italian pronunciation:[[doˈmeːniko moˈduɲɲo]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Italian "Help:IPA/Italian"); 9 January 1928 – 6 August 1994) was an Italian singer, songwriter, actor and, later in life, a member of the Italian Parliament. He is known for his 1958 international hit song "Nel blu dipinto di blu", for which he received the first Grammy Awards for Record of the Year and Song of the Year. He is considered the first Italian cantautore.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domenico_Modugno#cite_note-bio-1)

# Domenico Modugno
## Early life
[edit]
The youngest of four children, Modugno was born at Polignano a Mare, in the province of Bari (Apulia), on 9 January 1928.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domenico_Modugno#cite_note-Parents-2) His father, Vito Cosimo Modugno,[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domenico_Modugno#cite_note-Birth-3) was a municipal police commander,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domenico_Modugno#cite_note-Parents-2) while his mother, Pasqua Lorusso,[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domenico_Modugno#cite_note-Birth-3) was a housewife.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domenico_Modugno#cite_note-Parents-2)
At the age of 9, his family moved to San Pietro Vernotico, in the Province of Brindisi,[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domenico_Modugno#cite_note-4) where his father was transferred for a new job position.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domenico_Modugno#cite_note-5) Here Domenico attended primary school and learned San Pietro Vernotico's dialect, which belongs to the linguistic area of Salentino dialect, similar to Sicilian. He attended secondary school in Lecce.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domenico_Modugno#cite_note-bio-1)

While still studying, Modugno had a role in a cinematographic version of _Filumena Marturano_ by Eduardo De Filippo as well as some other films.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domenico_Modugno#cite_note-bio-1) In 1957, his song "Lazzarella", sung by Aurelio Fierro, came second in the Festival della Canzone Napoletana, bringing him his first taste of popularity.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domenico_Modugno#cite_note-bio-1)
In 1958, Modugno took part in Antonio Aniante's comedy _La Rosa di Zolfo_ at the Festival della Prosa in Venice. Also in 1958, he discovered the Italian comedy duo of Franco and Ciccio, became their manager and got them into a long-running film career.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domenico_Modugno#cite_note-6) The turning point of his career came in that year, when he also participated in the Sanremo Music Festival, presenting, together with Johnny Dorelli, the song "Nel blu dipinto di blu." Co-authored by Modugno and Franco Migliacci, the song won the contest and became an enormous success worldwide. It received two Grammy Awards[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domenico_Modugno#cite_note-NME_Rock_'N'_Roll_Years-7) with sales above 22 million copies, and represented Italy in the Eurovision Song Contest 1958, where it came in third.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domenico_Modugno#cite_note-bio-1)
Modugno reportedly used the money gained with "Nel blu dipinto di blu" to purchase a Ferrari; however, his car was totalled in an accident, which included his fenders being smashed. This was mentioned in the Allan Sherman song "America's a nice Italian Name".
texts.8:
# Domenico Modugno
## Career
In 1959, Modugno won the Sanremo Music Festival for the second time in a row, with "Piove" (also known as "Ciao, ciao bambina"), and received second place in 1960 with "Libero". This was a successful period of time for Modugno who again represented Italy in the Eurovision Song Contest of 1959. Later his hit song "Io" was sung by Elvis Presley in English with the title "Ask Me".[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domenico_Modugno#cite_note-bio-1)
In 1962, Modugno won the Sanremo Music Festival a third time with "Addio..., addio...." Four years later, he again represented Italy at Eurovision with "Dio, come ti amo". Sergio Franchi recorded it in Italian (titled "Oh How Much I Love You (Dio, come ti amo!)) on his 1967 RCA Victor album, _From Sergio-with Love_. Jack Jones recorded it in English for his 1967 album, _Our Song_, under the title "Oh How Much I Love You".[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domenico_Modugno#cite_note-bio-1)Shirley Bassey also recorded it with the title _Oh God How Much I Love You_, on her album _Keep the Music Playing_ in 1991.
Modugno was an actor in 44 movies (such as _Appuntamento a Ischia_), and was a film producer of two (_Tutto è musica_ of 1963 was his own biographical production).[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domenico_Modugno#cite_note-bio-1)
In 1970, Modugno focused on more classic music genres and profiles, as a singer and as a musician, adapting poetry, acting on television and in lead singing roles in modern operas.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domenico_Modugno#cite_note-bio-1)
texts.9:
# Domenico Modugno
## Final years
[edit]
In 1984, Modugno suffered a severe stroke and remained partially paralyzed; this forced him to abandon his artistic career and devote himself to rehab.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domenico_Modugno#cite_note-bio-1)
From 1986, he worked for the rights of disabled people, and in June 1987, he was elected congressman for Turin in the Italian Parliament, in the ranks of the Radical Party, a liberal-social political group.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domenico_Modugno#cite_note-bio-1) In the past, he had supported the campaigns of the Italian Socialist Party and one for divorce, in addition to criticizing the human rights violations by the regime of Augusto Pinochet, that cost him a denial of entry in Chile, where he had been scheduled to hold a concert.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domenico_Modugno#cite_note-bio-1) In this last stage of his life, instead, he was very active in social issues, fighting against the inhumane conditions of patients in the Agrigentopsychiatric hospital.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domenico_Modugno#cite_note-bio-1)
Modugno returned to the music scene, definitively (he already held a concert for former inmates of Agrigento's mental asylum, in 1989), in 1992–1993. His last song was _Delfini_ (_Dolphins_), in 1993 with his son, Massimo.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domenico_Modugno#cite_note-bio-1)

**Domenico Modugno** (born January 9, 1928 – died August 6, 1994) was a famous Italian singer, songwriter, and actor. Later in his life, he also became a member of the Italian Parliament. He is best known for his huge international hit song from 1958, "Nel blu dipinto di blu" (often called "Volare"). This song won him two Grammy Awards. Many people see him as the first true Italian _cantautore_, which means a singer-songwriter who writes and performs their own songs.

## Domenico Modugno's Early Life
Domenico Modugno was born in Polignano a Mare, Italy, on January 9, 1928. He was the youngest of four children. His father, Vito Cosimo Modugno, worked as a police commander, and his mother, Pasqua Lorusso, was a housewife.
When Domenico was nine, his family moved to San Pietro Vernotico. There, he went to primary school and learned the local dialect. He later attended secondary school in Lecce.
texts.3:
## Domenico Modugno's Music Career
While still a student, Domenico Modugno started acting in films. His first taste of fame came in 1957 when his song "Lazzarella" placed second in a big Italian music contest called the Festival della Canzone Napoletana.
The biggest moment of his career happened in 1958. He entered the Sanremo Music Festival with a song he co-wrote called "Nel blu dipinto di blu". This song won the contest and became a massive hit all over the world. It sold over 22 million copies and won two Grammy Awards. The song also represented Italy in the 1958 Eurovision Song Contest, where it finished third.
Domenico Modugno singing "Nel blu, dipinto di blu" at the Eurovision Song Contest 1958.
Modugno won the Sanremo Music Festival again in 1959 with "Piove" (also known as "Ciao, ciao bambina"). He also came in second place in 1960 with "Libero." He represented Italy in the Eurovision Song Contest again in 1959. Later, his song "Io" was covered by Elvis Presley in English, titled "Ask Me."
In 1962, Modugno won the Sanremo Music Festival for a third time with "Addio... addio...." He returned to Eurovision in 1966 with "Dio, come ti amo." Other artists like Sergio Franchi and Jack Jones later recorded this song.
Besides singing, Modugno acted in many movies, appearing in 44 films. He also produced two films, including _Tutto è musica_ (1963), which was about his own life. In the 1970s, he started focusing more on classical music and acting in modern operas.
texts.4:
## Domenico Modugno's Later Years
In 1984, Domenico Modugno had a serious health issue that affected his ability to perform. This led him to focus on his recovery.
From 1986, he became very active in fighting for the rights of people with disabilities. In June 1987, he was elected to the Italian Parliament as a representative for Turin. He was part of the Radical Party, a group focused on social issues. He spoke out against unfair treatment of patients in hospitals and supported campaigns for human rights.
Modugno returned to music in 1992–1993. His last song was "Delfini" (meaning "Dolphins"), which he sang with his son, Massimo, in 1993.
Domenico Modugno passed away on August 6, 1994, at the age of 66. He died from a heart attack at his home on the island of Lampedusa, south of Sicily. His beautiful beach house was later put up for sale.

# Domenico Modugno
**Domenico Modugno** (Italian pronunciation:[[doˈmeːniko moˈduɲɲo]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Italian "Help:IPA/Italian"); 9 January 1928 – 6 August 1994) was an Italian singer, songwriter, actor and, later in life, a member of the Italian Parliament. He is known for his 1958 international hit song "Nel blu dipinto di blu", for which he received the first Grammy Awards for Record of the Year and Song of the Year. He is considered the first Italian cantautore.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domenico_Modugno#cite_note-bio-1)

# Domenico Modugno
## Early life
[edit]
The youngest of four children, Modugno was born at Polignano a Mare, in the province of Bari (Apulia), on 9 January 1928.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domenico_Modugno#cite_note-Parents-2) His father, Vito Cosimo Modugno,[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domenico_Modugno#cite_note-Birth-3) was a municipal police commander,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domenico_Modugno#cite_note-Parents-2) while his mother, Pasqua Lorusso,[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domenico_Modugno#cite_note-Birth-3) was a housewife.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domenico_Modugno#cite_note-Parents-2)
At the age of 9, his family moved to San Pietro Vernotico, in the Province of Brindisi,[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domenico_Modugno#cite_note-4) where his father was transferred for a new job position.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domenico_Modugno#cite_note-5) Here Domenico attended primary school and learned San Pietro Vernotico's dialect, which belongs to the linguistic area of Salentino dialect, similar to Sicilian. He attended secondary school in Lecce.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domenico_Modugno#cite_note-bio-1)

# Domenico Modugno
## Career
[edit]
Modugno in 1955
[](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Modugno_durante_l'esibizione_al_Festival_di_sanremo_del_1958.jpg)
Modugno opens his arms while performing "Nel blu, dipinto di blu" (better known as "Volare") at the 1958 Sanremo Music Festival
While still studying, Modugno had a role in a cinematographic version of _Filumena Marturano_ by Eduardo De Filippo as well as some other films.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domenico_Modugno#cite_note-bio-1) In 1957, his song "Lazzarella", sung by Aurelio Fierro, came second in the Festival della Canzone Napoletana, bringing him his first taste of popularity.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domenico_Modugno#cite_note-bio-1)
In 1958, Modugno took part in Antonio Aniante's comedy _La Rosa di Zolfo_ at the Festival della Prosa in Venice. Also in 1958, he discovered the Italian comedy duo of Franco and Ciccio, became their manager and got them into a long-running film career.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domenico_Modugno#cite_note-6) The turning point of his career came in that year, when he also participated in the Sanremo Music Festival, presenting, together with Johnny Dorelli, the song "Nel blu dipinto di blu." Co-authored by Modugno and Franco Migliacci, the song won the contest and became an enormous success worldwide. It received two Grammy Awards[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domenico_Modugno#cite_note-NME_Rock_'N'_Roll_Years-7) with sales above 22 million copies, and represented Italy in the Eurovision Song Contest 1958, where it came in third.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domenico_Modugno#cite_note-bio-1)
Modugno reportedly used the money gained with "Nel blu dipinto di blu" to purchase a Ferrari; however, his car was totalled in an accident, which included his fenders being smashed. This was mentioned in the Allan Sherman song "America's a nice Italian Name".

# Domenico Modugno
## Career
In 1959, Modugno won the Sanremo Music Festival for the second time in a row, with "Piove" (also known as "Ciao, ciao bambina"), and received second place in 1960 with "Libero". This was a successful period of time for Modugno who again represented Italy in the Eurovision Song Contest of 1959. Later his hit song "Io" was sung by Elvis Presley in English with the title "Ask Me".[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domenico_Modugno#cite_note-bio-1)
In 1962, Modugno won the Sanremo Music Festival a third time with "Addio..., addio...." Four years later, he again represented Italy at Eurovision with "Dio, come ti amo". Sergio Franchi recorded it in Italian (titled "Oh How Much I Love You (Dio, come ti amo!)) on his 1967 RCA Victor album, _From Sergio-with Love_. Jack Jones recorded it in English for his 1967 album, _Our Song_, under the title "Oh How Much I Love You".[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domenico_Modugno#cite_note-bio-1)Shirley Bassey also recorded it with the title _Oh God How Much I Love You_, on her album _Keep the Music Playing_ in 1991.
Modugno was an actor in 44 movies (such as _Appuntamento a Ischia_), and was a film producer of two (_Tutto è musica_ of 1963 was his own biographical production).[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domenico_Modugno#cite_note-bio-1)
In 1970, Modugno focused on more classic music genres and profiles, as a singer and as a musician, adapting poetry, acting on television and in lead singing roles in modern operas.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domenico_Modugno#cite_note-bio-1)

# Domenico Modugno
## Final years
[edit]
In 1984, Modugno suffered a severe stroke and remained partially paralyzed; this forced him to abandon his artistic career and devote himself to rehab.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domenico_Modugno#cite_note-bio-1)
From 1986, he worked for the rights of disabled people, and in June 1987, he was elected congressman for Turin in the Italian Parliament, in the ranks of the Radical Party, a liberal-social political group.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domenico_Modugno#cite_note-bio-1) In the past, he had supported the campaigns of the Italian Socialist Party and one for divorce, in addition to criticizing the human rights violations by the regime of Augusto Pinochet, that cost him a denial of entry in Chile, where he had been scheduled to hold a concert.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domenico_Modugno#cite_note-bio-1) In this last stage of his life, instead, he was very active in social issues, fighting against the inhumane conditions of patients in the Agrigentopsychiatric hospital.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domenico_Modugno#cite_note-bio-1)
Modugno returned to the music scene, definitively (he already held a concert for former inmates of Agrigento's mental asylum, in 1989), in 1992–1993. His last song was _Delfini_ (_Dolphins_), in 1993 with his son, Massimo.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domenico_Modugno#cite_note-bio-1)

**Domenico Modugno** (born January 9, 1928 – died August 6, 1994) was a famous Italian singer, songwriter, and actor. Later in his life, he also became a member of the Italian Parliament. He is best known for his huge international hit song from 1958, "Nel blu dipinto di blu" (often called "Volare"). This song won him two Grammy Awards. Many people see him as the first true Italian _cantautore_, which means a singer-songwriter who writes and performs their own songs.

## Domenico Modugno's Early Life
Domenico Modugno was born in Polignano a Mare, Italy, on January 9, 1928. He was the youngest of four children. His father, Vito Cosimo Modugno, worked as a police commander, and his mother, Pasqua Lorusso, was a housewife.
When Domenico was nine, his family moved to San Pietro Vernotico. There, he went to primary school and learned the local dialect. He later attended secondary school in Lecce.

## Domenico Modugno's Music Career
While still a student, Domenico Modugno started acting in films. His first taste of fame came in 1957 when his song "Lazzarella" placed second in a big Italian music contest called the Festival della Canzone Napoletana.
The biggest moment of his career happened in 1958. He entered the Sanremo Music Festival with a song he co-wrote called "Nel blu dipinto di blu". This song won the contest and became a massive hit all over the world. It sold over 22 million copies and won two Grammy Awards. The song also represented Italy in the 1958 Eurovision Song Contest, where it finished third.
Domenico Modugno singing "Nel blu, dipinto di blu" at the Eurovision Song Contest 1958.
Modugno won the Sanremo Music Festival again in 1959 with "Piove" (also known as "Ciao, ciao bambina"). He also came in second place in 1960 with "Libero." He represented Italy in the Eurovision Song Contest again in 1959. Later, his song "Io" was covered by Elvis Presley in English, titled "Ask Me."
In 1962, Modugno won the Sanremo Music Festival for a third time with "Addio... addio...." He returned to Eurovision in 1966 with "Dio, come ti amo." Other artists like Sergio Franchi and Jack Jones later recorded this song.
Besides singing, Modugno acted in many movies, appearing in 44 films. He also produced two films, including _Tutto è musica_ (1963), which was about his own life. In the 1970s, he started focusing more on classical music and acting in modern operas.

## Domenico Modugno's Later Years
In 1984, Domenico Modugno had a serious health issue that affected his ability to perform. This led him to focus on his recovery.
From 1986, he became very active in fighting for the rights of people with disabilities. In June 1987, he was elected to the Italian Parliament as a representative for Turin. He was part of the Radical Party, a group focused on social issues. He spoke out against unfair treatment of patients in hospitals and supported campaigns for human rights.
Modugno returned to music in 1992–1993. His last song was "Delfini" (meaning "Dolphins"), which he sang with his son, Massimo, in 1993.
Domenico Modugno passed away on August 6, 1994, at the age of 66. He died from a heart attack at his home on the island of Lampedusa, south of Sicily. His beautiful beach house was later put up for sale.

Title: The Silver Comet: Althea Gibson
Chunks: 0,1,2,3,4,8,9,10,11,12
“Everything was white. The balls, the clothes, the socks, the shoes, the people. Ev-ery-thing.” The words of American tennis legend Billie Jean King. Back in a time when black players had to fight to make it to the court, they had to become pioneers to shatter the boundaries that oppressed. This is the world in which Althea Gibson was born into. And she fought so hard and won so much but today, her descendants are doing all they can to make this forgotten star of the court the legend she deserves to be. Shunned by the world of tennis, suffering horrendous abuse on the court, Althea should be a household name. She became Wimbledon’s first black champion and even met the Queen, one of the greatest tennis players who ever lived. Why has she been forgotten when she achieved more than Billie Jean King ever did? This is the remarkable story of her rise and fall…

##### Prologue
August 25 th, 1927. Althea was born in Silver, South Carolina, to Daniel and Annie Bell. They were sharecroppers on a cotton farm, but The Great Depression hit the south far harder than anywhere else. People fled poverty and misery and that’s just what Daniel and Annie did. In 1930, the family moved to Harlem. Althea may have been born in the Deep South rooted in slavery and exploitation, but now they were in the big city. 143 rd Street, between Lenox Avenue and Seventh Avenue. This was a world far removed from the cotton fields…
Harlem beckoned. 143 rd was designated a Police Athletic League play area – during daylight hours, it was barricaded so that the neighbourhood children could play sports in peace. It provided a welcome respite from the dark and cramped apartment Althea and her family called home, growing by the year as she was soon joined by three sisters and a brother. The street was virtually silent. Until the children came and suddenly, a buzz and hive of activity erupted so joyously, so wonderfully. But the sport that drew Althea in was paddle tennis. On the streets of Harlem, Althea shone. Two bats and a rubber sponge ball, a short net and a short court. This meant everything to Althea.
It was all she had because by 1940, her family life took a dark turn…

##### The Harlem Fighter
Her father was a fearsome man, teaching Althea how to box. But he was a violent man, too. Althea dropped out of school at 13 and almost immediately, she found herself in a shelter for abused children. Daniel was sent packing and so Annie and her five children were on their own, in Harlem, in a most difficult time. But Althea was not a weak child, far from it. She was tough. Imbued with a streetwise spirit borne from the fists of fury her father laid on her on the apartment rooftop, begging her to fight him. But he was gone now. And so Althea threw herself into the one thing she loved more than anything else. Her tennis.
Buddy Walker was the organiser of the play area and because this was the old days, he was also a bandleader and ran a bar. He spotted the precocious talent Althea had and he invited her to the Cosmopolitan Club, a private tennis club for the black people of Harlem. Rather wonderfully, the club’s only professional, Fred Johnson, took Althea on and started coaching her. He was a famous old man. Mainly because he was awesome at tennis and had only one arm.
Over time, Fred honed Althea’s talents and helped develop what was turning into a powerful serve of hers. This and her natural athleticism became hallmarks of her game. She was a troublemaker, a known truant and known to sleep on the subway to avoid going home, but her talent on the court spoke of a brighter future ahead. She was a blue collar kid. Whilst all the other players at the club tried to educate her and teach her all about etiquette, she had no desire in any of that and instead, focused solely on her game…
> I really wasn’t the tennis type [at first]. I kept wanting to fight the other player every time I started to lose a match.
She was rebellious, her unwillingness to compromise or cooperate changing slowly, slowly as time went by. Alongside her tennis, she also devoted herself to street fighting, watching movies and a basketball team named, The Mysterious Girls. She never recovered from her father’s savage beatings, but she worked hard and in 1939, she won the New York girl’s paddle ball championship. She was so good, she was made a junior member of the Cosmopolitan Club. Not bad going.

##### The Harlem Fighter
Because Althea was poor and her mother could hardly make ends meet, trying to find the funds to keep Althea in the club proved hard. But her neighbours adored her and, in 1940, they organised a collection in the area to help fund Althea’s ambitions. Hey kid, you got talent. Just cause you aint got money, doesn’t mean you aint going far in life. And things only got better and better. In 1941, she entered and won the American Tennis Association New York State Championship, her first tournament. Soon after, she won the ATA National Championship and through it all, she did it her way. Here Althea, a nice, tailored dress, as all ladies should wear on the court. What? I’m not wearing that! So she didn’t. She wore shorts and a collared shirt. And she cut her hair short. You’d be damned if you told her not to do something she set her heart on…
By 1947, she had won her first of 10 straight national ATA women’s titles. “I knew that I was an unusual, talented girl, through the Grace of God. I didn’t need to prove that to myself. I only wanted to prove it to my opponents.” Dr. Hubert Eaton and Dr. Robert Johnson were scholars with notable tennis ability, who nurtured promising, young black players. And they liked the look of Althea. This kid had talent. A lot of it. She astounded them. They went on to describe her as ‘combustible’ yet ‘highly skilful’. Which is a great way to sum up someone with Althea’s temperament.
Hubert and Robert thought that, in their hands, they had their very own Jackie Robinson, an athlete who broke down racial barriers. They were worried, however, that her lack of education would hamper her progress. So they hatched a plan. Althea would live and train with Robert in Wilmington, North Carolina. Robert and Hubert were civil rights organisers, their plan? To create the first black tennis champion.
Althea was their charge…

##### The American Fighter
Racial segregation in America stopped black Americans mixing with their white counterparts in many aspects of life, from education to employment and transportation. The divide also existed in tennis, which is why Althea was so important to her new mentors. Black players were not allowed to compete in the US National Championships, forming the ATA so they could hold their own tournament. But Hubert and Robert didn’t want this to go on. They wanted a black player who could integrate the all-white US Lawn Tennis competitions. The times were changing and they were changing rapidly.
In 1950, reigning national champion Alice Marble wrote a magazine article scathing in tone challenging the all-white stance in tennis. The big question on everyone’s lips… would this rising star of the tennis world, Althea, be allowed to compete? Alice wrote, ‘I think it is time we faced a few facts. If tennis is a game for ladies and gentlemen, it is time we acted a little more like gentle people and less like sanctimonious hypocrites.’ Oof, that’s gotta hurt. It worked. The white men in charge backed down. Under increasing pressure, they relented and allowed Althea to play. This was a momentous moment in history and makes it all the sadder than Althea has been forgotten…
Althea became the first black player to receive an invitation to the US National Championships. On her 23 rd birthday, she made her Forest Hills debut. Sadly, she lost, but only just, in the second round in a rain hit, three-set match, but credit to Althea, she lost to the reigning Wimbledon champion. During the match, one of 11 stone eagles perched on the top of the stadium in Queens was struck by lightning, sent crashing to the floor, leading to the match being abandoned. It ruined and overshadowed Althea’s maiden appearance.
Play resumed the next day but Althea was shaken by the ordeal. Even worse, during the match, the watching crowd hurled abuse at her. They shouted to her opponent, “Beat the n*****! Beat the n*****!” Althea was a tough woman but she was, as you can imagine, really upset. She was beaten in just 11 minutes. The coverage the match received was truly international, truly sensational. Journalist Lester Rodney wrote:

##### The Wimbledon Glory
She was named Female Athlete of the Year and became the first black woman to appear on the covers of Sports Illustrated and Time. So why has she been forgotten? Because, sadly, adulation does not last forever…

##### The End of the Amateur
Having won 56 national and international singles and doubles titles, Althea retired from amateur tennis in 1958. Well, go out with a bang, as they say. She was making no money from it. “Being the Queen of Tennis is all well and good,” she said, “but you can’t eat a crown. Nor can you send the Internal Revenue Service a throne clipped to their tax forms. The landlord and the grocer are funny that way.” She started playing exhibition matches in 1959 to make ends meet, but in that year, the greatest female tennis player on Earth only made $500 in prize money. It just wasn’t enough. So she became a saxophonist.
Well, she liked the saxophone and she could sing, she long harboured a dream to be in the entertainment biz. She was very talented at many things. She made her professional singing debut at W.C. Handy’s 84 th birthday tribute at the Waldorf Astoria Hotel. An executive from Dot Records was so impressed her signed her up to a record deal. Yes, you’re right, this is the most abrupt gear change in history…
‘Althea Gibson Sings’ was released in 1959 and I tell you what, she had a glorious set of pipes on her. My heavens, what a voice. She performed on The Ed Sullivan show but sales were poor. She appeared on the panel show, ‘What’s My Line?’ and even appeared in the 1959 movie, The Horse Soldiers. She could do, literally, _anything_. She also worked as a sports commentator, appeared in print and television advertisements and became involved in social issues and community activities. She even published her first memoir.
Her tennis career, meanwhile, was sinking fast. “When I looked around me, I saw that white tennis players, some of whom I had thrashed on the court, were picking up offers and invitations. Suddenly, it dawned on me that my triumphs had not destroyed the racial barriers once and for all, as I had – perhaps naïvely – hoped. Or if I did destroy them, they had been erected behind me again.” She was becoming forlorn.

##### The End of the Amateur
If you’re ready for another abrupt gear change, in 1964, she became the first black woman to join the Ladies Professional Golf Association. Yup. Even then, she suffered abuse for the colour of her skin. Nowhere would let her compete. Even the places that did would not let her use their changing facilities so she was forced to change in her car. Her earnings from her brief golf career was just $25,000. She made ends meet with sponsorship deals but her life was falling apart. She married the brother of her best friend in 1965 and he did all he could to support Althea. But she was struggling.
Was she good at golf? Of course she was. Great tennis player, great singer and at golf, she broke many course records. Her highest ranking was an impressive 27 th, her tournament best a tie for second. She continued to appear on television panel shows, too, but she retired from golf in 1978. She tried to enter major tennis tournaments again with the advent of the Open Era but she was just too old to compete against the younger players. A golf comeback in 1987 at the age of 60 was met with similar disappointment.
Life was tough for Althea. And it was about to get worse…

##### The Downfall
It’s really important to remember that Althea was a good person but she was living a time where black people and women were treated even worse than they are now and were given no real support, even women like Althea, who had achieved so much and today, would be a revered legend. She was sad. Her aspirations of later years unfulfilled and efforts to reach out for endorsements met with closed doors. She started community projects in association with Pepsi, bringing portable nets and equipment to underprivileged areas across America and helped to run many tennis outreach projects. She coached, too, but in the late 1980s, disaster struck when she suffered two cerebral haemorrhages, followed by a stroke in 1992. She was broke. Once the greatest tennis player of them all, she had no money to her name. She did the best she could. But it wasn’t enough.
She could not afford her medical expenses so she reached out various tennis organisations. She thought that because of her fame in the tennis world that they might care for their former pros. The people who brought tennis to life. No. All the major tennis organisations wanted nothing to do with Althea. She had no husband, having divorced twice in her life, no children and few friends. It was so unfair. She didn’t deserve any of this.
But she had support. In her darkest hour, her fellow tennis professionals rallied around and raised nearly $1 million for her healthcare. She had drifted away from the sport but never too far from the limelight. But her name gradually became lost as a wave of new black female superstars rose up in the game of tennis. But Althea was the first. Even today, in Harlem, few have heard of her. In her life, she never got the notoriety she really deserved, especially in her later years. And it all came to a head in 1995.

##### The Downfall
Suffering from extreme poverty, she found herself living alone in New Jersey. She was very sick and all hope seemed lost. She called an old friend. “I’m just calling to say goodbye,” she said. She was going to kill herself. And I know it’s easy to be mad at people who want to end it all, but don’t think that for Althea. She had fallen on hard times and she didn’t deserve any of that. She should have been a celebrity. But now she had lost everything.
And once more, the tennis world, not the officials because they didn’t care, but the players, they rallied around. Come on, Althea. You are so loved. You are brilliant and amazing and wonderful, come on. You’re one of the greats. They raised so much money for her. It pulled her from the brink. She was comfortable. She felt a renewed sense of happiness and wellbeing. From a difficult childhood, to a glorious adulthood, to the dark and troubled waters of her old age, Althea was at peace once more. She felt something remarkable. She felt the love that she had earned by, simply put, being one of the all-time greats.
We lost her not that long ago. In 2003, she had a heart attack but survived, but later that year, due to complications from respiratory and bladder infections, she passed away, on September 28 th. She was 76. A star of the court, forgotten, but, thankfully, in recent years, the fight is on to get her the recognition she so clearly deserves…

## [PDF page 4]
Wayne's family moved to Palmdale, California, and then in 1916 to Glendale, California, where  
his  father  worked  as  a  pharmacist.  A  local  fireman  at  the  station  on  his  route  to  school  in  
Glendale  started  calling  him  "Little  Duke"  because  he  never  went  anywhere  without  his  
huge Airedale Terrier, Duke. He preferred "Duke" to "Marion," and the nickname stuck. Wayne  
attended Wilson Middle School in Glendale. As a teen, he worked in an ice cream shop for a  
man who shod horses for Hollywood studios. He was also active as a member of the Order of  
DeMolay,  a  youth  organization  of  the Freemasons.  He  played  football  for  the  1924  league  
champion Glendale High School team.

## [PDF page 4]
Wayne  applied  to  the U.S.  Naval  Academy,  but  he  was  not  accepted.  He  instead  attended  
the University  of  Southern  California (USC),  majoring  in pre-law.  He  was  a  member  of  
the Trojan  Knights and Sigma  Chi fraternities. Wayne  also  played  on  the USC  football  
team under Coach Howard Jones. A broken collarbone injury curtailed his athletic career; He  
lost his athletic scholarship, and without funds, had to leave the university.  
As a favor to USC football  Coach Howard Jones, who had given silent western film star Tom  
Mix tickets to USC games, director John Ford and Mix hired Wayne as a prop boy and extra.  
Wayne  later  credited  his  walk,  talk,  and  persona to  his  acquaintance  with Wyatt  Earp,  who  
was  good  friends  with  Tom  Mix. Wayne  soon  moved  to bit  parts,  establishing  a  longtime  
friendship with the director who provided most of those roles, John Ford. Early in this period,  
he had a minor, uncredited role as a guard in the 1926 film Bardelys the Magnificent. Wayne  
also  appeared  with  his  USC  teammates  playing  football  in Brown  of  Harvard (1926), The  
Dropkick (1927), and Salute (1929) and Columbia's Maker of Men (filmed in 1930, released in  
1931). While working for Fox Film Corporation in bit roles, Wayne was given on-screen credit  
as "Duke Morrison" only once, in Words and Music in 1929.  
Initially  working  for  Fox,  he mostly  appeared  in  small  bit  parts. His  first  leading  role  came  
in Raoul  Walsh's  lavish widescreen epic The  Big  Trail in  1930,  which  led  to  leading  roles in  
numerous B  movies throughout  the  1930’s,  many  of  them  in  the western genre. Walsh  saw  

## [PDF page 4]
him moving studio furniture while working as a prop boy and cast him in his first starring role  
in The Big Trail. For his screen name, Walsh suggested "Anthony Wayne", after Revolutionary  
War general "Mad" Anthony Wayne. Fox Studios chief Winfield Sheehan rejected it as sounding  
"too  Italian."  Walsh  then  suggested  "John  Wayne."  Sheehan  agreed,  and  the  name  was  set.  
Wayne was not even present for the discussion.  
Wayne's  career  took  off  in  1939,  with John  Ford's Stagecoach making  him  an  instant  
mainstream star. Wayne went on to star in 142 pictures. Biographer Ronald Davis says: "John  
Wayne personified for millions the nation's frontier heritage. Eighty-three of his movies were  
westerns  and  in  them  he  played  cowboys,  cavalrymen  and  unconquerable  loners  extracted  
from the Republic's central creation myth."  
Wayne's  first  color  film  was Shepherd  of  the  Hills (1941),  in  which  he  co-starred  with  his  
longtime friend Harry Carey. Wayne was exempted from service in World War II due to his age  
(34  at  the  time  of  Pearl  Harbor)  and  family  status,  classified  as  3-A  (family  
deferment). Despite  his  desire  to  serve,  Republic  Pictures  thought  he  was  too  valuable  to  
expose to danger in the War. Wayne toured U.S. bases and hospitals in the South Pacific for  
three months in 1943 and 1944 with the USO.
4

## [PDF page 5]
John Wayne – America’s Cowboy
The  following  year,  Wayne  appeared in  his  only  
film  directed  by Cecil  B.  DeMille,  the  Techni-  
color epic Reap  the Wild  Wind  (1942),  in  which  
he co-starred with Ray Milland; it was one of the  
rare  times  he  played  a  character  with  
questionable  values.  He  would  appear  in  more  
than 20 of John Ford's films throughout the next  
two decades.  
Wayne's other well-known western roles include  
a  cattleman  driving  his  herd  north  on  
the Chisholm  Trail in  Red  River (1948);  She  
Wore a Yellow Ribbon (1949); he also played the  
part of a Civil War veteran whose young niece is  
abducted  by  a  tribe  of Comanches in The  
Searchers (1956);  and  a  troubled  rancher  
competing with an Eastern lawyer for a woman's  
hand  in  marriage in The  Man  Who  Shot  Liberty  
Valance (1962)  with  James  Stewart:  the  first  
movie in which he called someone "Pilgrim."  
He is also remembered for his roles in The Quiet  
Man (1952), The  Wings  of  Eagles (1957),  Rio  
Bravo (1959) and The Longest Day (1962). In his  
final screen performance, he starred as an aging gunfighter battling cancer in The Shootist in  
1976.  He  appeared  with  many  important  Hollywood  stars  of  his  era,  and  his  last  public  
appearance was at the Academy Awards ceremony on April 9, 1979.  
Wayne  was married  three  times  and  divorced  twice.  He  was  fluent  in  Spanish  and  his  three  
wives  were  each  of  Hispanic descent.  Several  of  Wayne's  children  entered  the  film  and  
television industry; Michael Wayne and Patrick Wayne appeared in several movies with their  

## [PDF page 5]
father; Wayne's son Ethan was billed as John Ethan Wayne in a few films.  
Wayne's hair began thinning in the 1940’s, and he started wearing a hairpiece by the end of  
that  decade.  He  had  been  a  chain  smoker  of  cigarettes  since  young  adulthood  and  was  
diagnosed with lung cancer in 1964. He underwent successful surgery to remove his entire left  
lung and four  ribs. Five years later, Wayne was declared cancer-free. Wayne died of stomach  
cancer on  June  11,  1979,  at  the UCLA  Medical  Center,  and  was  interred  in  the  Pacific  View  
Memorial Park cemetery in Corona del Mar, Newport Beach.
5

## [PDF page 7]
in  the Los  Angeles  Herald-Examiner that  read,  "Yodeler  for  old-time  act,  to  travel.  Tenor  
preferred."  Although  Nolan  stayed  with  the  group  only  a  short  time,  he  and  Len  stayed in  
touch. Nolan was replaced by Tim Spencer.  
In the spring of 1932, Len Slye, Spencer, and another singer, Slumber Nichols, left the Rocky  
Mountaineers to form a trio, which soon failed. Throughout that year, Len and Tim Spencer  
moved through a series of short-lived groups, including the International Cowboys and the O-  
Bar-O  Cowboys.  When  Spencer  left  the  O-Bar-O  Cowboys  to  take a  break  from  music,  Len  
joined Jack LeFevre and His Texas Outlaws, who were a popular act on a local Los Angeles  
radio station.  In 1932 a palomino colt foaled in California was named "Golden Cloud"; when  
Len acquired him, he renamed him "Trigger."  
In 1932, Len met an admirer named Lucile Ascolese. Roy and Lucile were married in 1933 by  
a justice of the peace in Los Angeles. The marriage was a failure, and the couple divorced in  
1936.

## [PDF page 7]
In early 1933, Len Slye, with Bob Nolan, and Tim Spencer formed a group called the Pioneers  
Trio,  with  Slye  on  guitar,  Nolan  on  string  bass  and  Spencer  on  lead  vocals.  The  three  
rehearsed for weeks refining their vocal harmonies. During this time, Slye continued to work  
with  his  radio  singing group,  while  Spencer  and  Nolan began  writing  songs  for  the  trio.  In  
early 1934, fiddle player Hugh Farr joined the group, adding a bass voice to the group's vocal  
arrangements.  Later  that  year,  the  Pioneers  Trio  became  the Sons  of  the  Pioneers when  a  
radio  station  announcer  changed  their  name  because  he  felt  they  were  too  young  to  be  
"pioneers." The name was received well and fit the group, who were no longer a trio.  
By the summer of 1934, the popularity and fame of the Sons of the Pioneers extended beyond  
the  Los  Angeles  area  and  quickly  spread  across  the  country  through  short  syndicated  radio  
segments  that  were  later  rebroadcast  across  the  United  States.  After  signing  a  recording  
contract  with  the  newly  founded Decca label,  the  Sons  of  the  Pioneers  made  their  first  
commercial recording on August 8, 1934.
7

## [PDF page 8]
Sons of the Pioneers  
One  of  the  first  songs  recorded  by  the  group  during  that  first  August  session  was  "Tumbling  
Tumbleweeds"  written  by  Bob  Nolan.  Over  the  next  two  years  the  Sons  of  the  Pioneers  would  
record 32 songs for Decca, including the classic "Cool Water."  
While  on  tour  with  the  "O-Bar-O  Cowboys"  in  June  1933  Len  met  Grace  Arline  Wilkins  at  
a Roswell, New Mexico radio station. They were married three years later in Roswell on June 11,  
1936 after having corresponded since their first meeting.  
From his first film appearance in 1935, Rogers worked steadily in western films, including a large  
supporting role as a singing cowboy while still billed as "Leonard Slye" in a  Gene Autry movie. In  
1938,  when  Autry  was demanding  more money  for  his  work,  Slye  was  immediately  rechristened  
"Roy  Rogers."  Actually,  there  was  a  competition  for  a  new  singing  cowboy,  and  many  western  
singers  sought  the  job,  including  Willie  Phelps  of  the  Phelps  brothers  who  appeared  in  early  
western movies. Slye ended up winning the contest and became Roy Rogers.  
Slye's stage name was suggested by Republic Picture's staff after Will Rogers and the shortening of  
Leroy  and  he  was  assigned  the  lead  in Under  Western  Stars.  Rogers  became  a  matinee  idol  and  
American  legend.  A  competitor  for  Gene  Autry  as  the  nation's  favorite singing  cowboy was  
suddenly  born.  In  addition  to  his  own  movies,  Rogers  played  a  supporting  role  in  the John  
Wayne classic Dark  Command (1940).  Rogers  became  a  major  box  office  attraction.  Unlike  other  

## [PDF page 8]
stars, the vast majority of Rogers' leading roles allowed him to play a character with his own name  
in the manner of Gene Autry.  
In 1941, Len and Grace adopted a daughter, Cheryl Darlene. Two years later, Grace gave birth to  
the couple's daughter Linda Lou, followed by son Roy, Jr. ("Dusty") in 1946. Grace Arline Wilkins  
died of complications from the birth a few days later, on November 3.  
Rogers met Dale Evans in 1944 when they were cast in a film together. They fell in love soon after  
Arline's death and Rogers proposed to her during a rodeo at Chicago Stadium. They married on New  
Year's  Eve  in  1947  at  the  Flying  L  Ranch  in Davis,  Oklahoma,  where  they  had  filmed Home  in  
Oklahoma a  few  months  earlier.  Together  they  had  five  children  including  Robin  Elizabeth, who  
had Down syndrome and died of complications with mumps shortly before her second birthday.  
Rogers  and  Evans's  famous  theme  song,  "Happy  Trails",  was  written  by  Evans;  they  sang  it as  a  
duet to sign off their television show. In the fall of 1962, the couple co-hosted a comedy-western-  
variety program, The Roy Rogers and Dale Evans Show, which aired on ABC. It was cancelled after  
three months, losing in the ratings to The Jackie Gleason Show on CBS. Roy also made numerous  
cameo or guest appearances on other popular television shows, starring as himself or other cowboy-  
type  characters,  such  as  in  an  episode  of Wonder  Woman called  "The  Bushwackers".  Rogers  also  
owned  a  Hollywood  production  company  which  handled  his  own  series.  It  also  filmed  other  
undertakings, including the 1955–1956 CBS western series Brave Eagle starring Keith Larsen as a  
young  peaceful  Cheyenne chief.  In  1968,  Rogers  licensed  his  name  to  the  Marriott  corporation,  

## [PDF page 8]
which converted its Hot Shoppes locations to Roy Rogers Restaurants, with which Rogers otherwise  
had no involvement.  
When  Rogers  died  of congestive  heart  failure on  July  6,  1998,  he  was  residing  in Apple  Valley,  
California.  He  was  buried  at  Sunset  Hills  Memorial  Park  in  Apple  Valley,  as  was  his  wife, Dale  
Evans, three years later.
8

## [PDF page 4]
Wayne's family moved to Palmdale, California, and then in 1916 to Glendale, California, where  
his  father  worked  as  a  pharmacist.  A  local  fireman  at  the  station  on  his  route  to  school  in  
Glendale  started  calling  him  "Little  Duke"  because  he  never  went  anywhere  without  his  
huge Airedale Terrier, Duke. He preferred "Duke" to "Marion," and the nickname stuck. Wayne  
attended Wilson Middle School in Glendale. As a teen, he worked in an ice cream shop for a  
man who shod horses for Hollywood studios. He was also active as a member of the Order of  
DeMolay,  a  youth  organization  of  the Freemasons.  He  played  football  for  the  1924  league  
champion Glendale High School team.
texts.6:
## [PDF page 4]
Wayne  applied  to  the U.S.  Naval  Academy,  but  he  was  not  accepted.  He  instead  attended  
the University  of  Southern  California (USC),  majoring  in pre-law.  He  was  a  member  of  
the Trojan  Knights and Sigma  Chi fraternities. Wayne  also  played  on  the USC  football  
team under Coach Howard Jones. A broken collarbone injury curtailed his athletic career; He  
lost his athletic scholarship, and without funds, had to leave the university.  
As a favor to USC football  Coach Howard Jones, who had given silent western film star Tom  
Mix tickets to USC games, director John Ford and Mix hired Wayne as a prop boy and extra.  
Wayne  later  credited  his  walk,  talk,  and  persona to  his  acquaintance  with Wyatt  Earp,  who  
was  good  friends  with  Tom  Mix. Wayne  soon  moved  to bit  parts,  establishing  a  longtime  
friendship with the director who provided most of those roles, John Ford. Early in this period,  
he had a minor, uncredited role as a guard in the 1926 film Bardelys the Magnificent. Wayne  
also  appeared  with  his  USC  teammates  playing  football  in Brown  of  Harvard (1926), The  
Dropkick (1927), and Salute (1929) and Columbia's Maker of Men (filmed in 1930, released in  
1931). While working for Fox Film Corporation in bit roles, Wayne was given on-screen credit  
as "Duke Morrison" only once, in Words and Music in 1929.  
Initially  working  for  Fox,  he mostly  appeared  in  small  bit  parts. His  first  leading  role  came  
in Raoul  Walsh's  lavish widescreen epic The  Big  Trail in  1930,  which  led  to  leading  roles in  
numerous B  movies throughout  the  1930’s,  many  of  them  in  the western genre. Walsh  saw
texts.7:
## [PDF page 4]
him moving studio furniture while working as a prop boy and cast him in his first starring role  
in The Big Trail. For his screen name, Walsh suggested "Anthony Wayne", after Revolutionary  
War general "Mad" Anthony Wayne. Fox Studios chief Winfield Sheehan rejected it as sounding  
"too  Italian."  Walsh  then  suggested  "John  Wayne."  Sheehan  agreed,  and  the  name  was  set.  
Wayne was not even present for the discussion.  
Wayne's  career  took  off  in  1939,  with John  Ford's Stagecoach making  him  an  instant  
mainstream star. Wayne went on to star in 142 pictures. Biographer Ronald Davis says: "John  
Wayne personified for millions the nation's frontier heritage. Eighty-three of his movies were  
westerns  and  in  them  he  played  cowboys,  cavalrymen  and  unconquerable  loners  extracted  
from the Republic's central creation myth."  
Wayne's  first  color  film  was Shepherd  of  the  Hills (1941),  in  which  he  co-starred  with  his  
longtime friend Harry Carey. Wayne was exempted from service in World War II due to his age  
(34  at  the  time  of  Pearl  Harbor)  and  family  status,  classified  as  3-A  (family  
deferment). Despite  his  desire  to  serve,  Republic  Pictures  thought  he  was  too  valuable  to  
expose to danger in the War. Wayne toured U.S. bases and hospitals in the South Pacific for  
three months in 1943 and 1944 with the USO.

texts.8:
## [PDF page 5]
John Wayne – America’s Cowboy
The  following  year,  Wayne  appeared in  his  only  
film  directed  by Cecil  B.  DeMille,  the  Techni-  
color epic Reap  the Wild  Wind  (1942),  in  which  
he co-starred with Ray Milland; it was one of the  
rare  times  he  played  a  character  with  
questionable  values.  He  would  appear  in  more  
than 20 of John Ford's films throughout the next  
two decades.  
Wayne's other well-known western roles include  
a  cattleman  driving  his  herd  north  on  
the Chisholm  Trail in  Red  River (1948);  She  
Wore a Yellow Ribbon (1949); he also played the  
part of a Civil War veteran whose young niece is  
abducted  by  a  tribe  of Comanches in The  
Searchers (1956);  and  a  troubled  rancher  
competing with an Eastern lawyer for a woman's  
hand  in  marriage in The  Man  Who  Shot  Liberty  
Valance (1962)  with  James  Stewart:  the  first  
movie in which he called someone "Pilgrim."  
He is also remembered for his roles in The Quiet  
Man (1952), The  Wings  of  Eagles (1957),  Rio  
Bravo (1959) and The Longest Day (1962). In his  
final screen performance, he starred as an aging gunfighter battling cancer in The Shootist in  
1976.  He  appeared  with  many  important  Hollywood  stars  of  his  era,  and  his  last  public  
appearance was at the Academy Awards ceremony on April 9, 1979.  
Wayne  was married  three  times  and  divorced  twice.  He  was  fluent  in  Spanish  and  his  three  
wives  were  each  of  Hispanic descent.  Several  of  Wayne's  children  entered  the  film  and  
television industry; Michael Wayne and Patrick Wayne appeared in several movies with their
texts.9:
## [PDF page 5]
father; Wayne's son Ethan was billed as John Ethan Wayne in a few films.  
Wayne's hair began thinning in the 1940’s, and he started wearing a hairpiece by the end of  
that  decade.  He  had  been  a  chain  smoker  of  cigarettes  since  young  adulthood  and  was  
diagnosed with lung cancer in 1964. He underwent successful surgery to remove his entire left  
lung and four  ribs. Five years later, Wayne was declared cancer-free. Wayne died of stomach  
cancer on  June  11,  1979,  at  the UCLA  Medical  Center,  and  was  interred  in  the  Pacific  View  
Memorial Park cemetery in Corona del Mar, Newport Beach.

texts.13:
## [PDF page 7]
in  the Los  Angeles  Herald-Examiner that  read,  "Yodeler  for  old-time  act,  to  travel.  Tenor  
preferred."  Although  Nolan  stayed  with  the  group  only  a  short  time,  he  and  Len  stayed in  
touch. Nolan was replaced by Tim Spencer.  
In the spring of 1932, Len Slye, Spencer, and another singer, Slumber Nichols, left the Rocky  
Mountaineers to form a trio, which soon failed. Throughout that year, Len and Tim Spencer  
moved through a series of short-lived groups, including the International Cowboys and the O-  
Bar-O  Cowboys.  When  Spencer  left  the  O-Bar-O  Cowboys  to  take a  break  from  music,  Len  
joined Jack LeFevre and His Texas Outlaws, who were a popular act on a local Los Angeles  
radio station.  In 1932 a palomino colt foaled in California was named "Golden Cloud"; when  
Len acquired him, he renamed him "Trigger."  
In 1932, Len met an admirer named Lucile Ascolese. Roy and Lucile were married in 1933 by  
a justice of the peace in Los Angeles. The marriage was a failure, and the couple divorced in  
1936.
texts.14:
## [PDF page 7]
In early 1933, Len Slye, with Bob Nolan, and Tim Spencer formed a group called the Pioneers  
Trio,  with  Slye  on  guitar,  Nolan  on  string  bass  and  Spencer  on  lead  vocals.  The  three  
rehearsed for weeks refining their vocal harmonies. During this time, Slye continued to work  
with  his  radio  singing group,  while  Spencer  and  Nolan began  writing  songs  for  the  trio.  In  
early 1934, fiddle player Hugh Farr joined the group, adding a bass voice to the group's vocal  
arrangements.  Later  that  year,  the  Pioneers  Trio  became  the Sons  of  the  Pioneers when  a  
radio  station  announcer  changed  their  name  because  he  felt  they  were  too  young  to  be  
"pioneers." The name was received well and fit the group, who were no longer a trio.  
By the summer of 1934, the popularity and fame of the Sons of the Pioneers extended beyond  
the  Los  Angeles  area  and  quickly  spread  across  the  country  through  short  syndicated  radio  
segments  that  were  later  rebroadcast  across  the  United  States.  After  signing  a  recording  
contract  with  the  newly  founded Decca label,  the  Sons  of  the  Pioneers  made  their  first  
commercial recording on August 8, 1934.
7
texts.15:
## [PDF page 8]
Sons of the Pioneers  
One  of  the  first  songs  recorded  by  the  group  during  that  first  August  session  was  "Tumbling  
Tumbleweeds"  written  by  Bob  Nolan.  Over  the  next  two  years  the  Sons  of  the  Pioneers  would  
record 32 songs for Decca, including the classic "Cool Water."  
While  on  tour  with  the  "O-Bar-O  Cowboys"  in  June  1933  Len  met  Grace  Arline  Wilkins  at  
a Roswell, New Mexico radio station. They were married three years later in Roswell on June 11,  
1936 after having corresponded since their first meeting.  
From his first film appearance in 1935, Rogers worked steadily in western films, including a large  
supporting role as a singing cowboy while still billed as "Leonard Slye" in a  Gene Autry movie. In  
1938,  when  Autry  was demanding  more money  for  his  work,  Slye  was  immediately  rechristened  
"Roy  Rogers."  Actually,  there  was  a  competition  for  a  new  singing  cowboy,  and  many  western  
singers  sought  the  job,  including  Willie  Phelps  of  the  Phelps  brothers  who  appeared  in  early  
western movies. Slye ended up winning the contest and became Roy Rogers.  
Slye's stage name was suggested by Republic Picture's staff after Will Rogers and the shortening of  
Leroy  and  he  was  assigned  the  lead  in Under  Western  Stars.  Rogers  became  a  matinee  idol  and  
American  legend.  A  competitor  for  Gene  Autry  as  the  nation's  favorite singing  cowboy was  
suddenly  born.  In  addition  to  his  own  movies,  Rogers  played  a  supporting  role  in  the John  
Wayne classic Dark  Command (1940).  Rogers  became  a  major  box  office  attraction.  Unlike  other
texts.16:
## [PDF page 8]
stars, the vast majority of Rogers' leading roles allowed him to play a character with his own name  
in the manner of Gene Autry.  
In 1941, Len and Grace adopted a daughter, Cheryl Darlene. Two years later, Grace gave birth to  
the couple's daughter Linda Lou, followed by son Roy, Jr. ("Dusty") in 1946. Grace Arline Wilkins  
died of complications from the birth a few days later, on November 3.  
Rogers met Dale Evans in 1944 when they were cast in a film together. They fell in love soon after  
Arline's death and Rogers proposed to her during a rodeo at Chicago Stadium. They married on New  
Year's  Eve  in  1947  at  the  Flying  L  Ranch  in Davis,  Oklahoma,  where  they  had  filmed Home  in  
Oklahoma a  few  months  earlier.  Together  they  had  five  children  including  Robin  Elizabeth, who  
had Down syndrome and died of complications with mumps shortly before her second birthday.  
Rogers  and  Evans's  famous  theme  song,  "Happy  Trails",  was  written  by  Evans;  they  sang  it as  a  
duet to sign off their television show. In the fall of 1962, the couple co-hosted a comedy-western-  
variety program, The Roy Rogers and Dale Evans Show, which aired on ABC. It was cancelled after  
three months, losing in the ratings to The Jackie Gleason Show on CBS. Roy also made numerous  
cameo or guest appearances on other popular television shows, starring as himself or other cowboy-  
type  characters,  such  as  in  an  episode  of Wonder  Woman called  "The  Bushwackers".  Rogers  also  
owned  a  Hollywood  production  company  which  handled  his  own  series.  It  also  filmed  other  
undertakings, including the 1955–1956 CBS western series Brave Eagle starring Keith Larsen as a  
young  peaceful  Cheyenne chief.  In  1968,  Rogers  licensed  his  name  to  the  Marriott  corporation,
texts.17:
## [PDF page 8]
which converted its Hot Shoppes locations to Roy Rogers Restaurants, with which Rogers otherwise  
had no involvement.  
When  Rogers  died  of congestive  heart  failure on  July  6,  1998,  he  was  residing  in Apple  Valley,  
California.  He  was  buried  at  Sunset  Hills  Memorial  Park  in  Apple  Valley,  as  was  his  wife, Dale  
Evans, three years later.
